October 2026
Abstract

This paper provides moment conditions for dynamic multinomial logit panel data models with individual specific fixed effects. The moment conditions do not depend on the fixed effects and thus form the basis for generalized method of moments estimation. For a leading case, we provide sufficient conditions under which the moment conditions identify the common parameters, and we illustrate their use in an empirical application to household soft drink purchases. The construction of moment conditions is based on transformed models obtained by permuting outcomes across time periods. For any cyclic permutation, the ratio of the transformed model probability to the true model probability is free of the fixed effects, and comparing two such ratios yields restrictions on the common parameters of interest. This construction is not specific to the multinomial logit. It applies to any dynamic panel data model whose static counterpart admits a symmetric sufficient statistic for the fixed effects. This unifies our main result with analogous results for other models.

1 Introduction

Controlling for individual heterogeneity without imposing strong assumptions on its relationship to observed covariates is a central challenge in the econometric analysis of nonlinear panel data models. Suppose the individual-specific effects are treated as parameters and estimated jointly with the common parameters of interest. The resulting estimator is then generally inconsistent as the number of cross-sectional units grows with the number of time periods held fixed. This is the classical incidental parameter problem (Neyman and Scott, 1948). This paper studies the dynamic multinomial logit model for panel data with fixed effects. Our main contribution is to construct moment conditions that depend on the common parameters but not on the individual-specific effects. We obtain them from a transformed model that permutes outcomes across time periods, and that cancels the fixed effects through the structure of the multinomial logit likelihood.

One approach to panel data discrete choice models with fixed effects is to look for sufficient statistics for the fixed effects. It dates back to Rasch (1960), who observed that in a binary logit model with strictly exogenous regressors the sum of an individual’s outcomes is a sufficient statistic for the fixed effect, so that conditional maximum likelihood can be used. Chamberlain (1980) extended this to the static multinomial logit, where the vector of choice frequencies is sufficient for the fixed effects, and Magnac (2000) obtained an analogous result when the only regressors are lagged dependent variables. Unfortunately, conditional likelihood methods generally break down in the empirically most relevant case in which both lagged dependent variables and strictly exogenous regressors are present. Honoré and Kyriazidou (2000) handled this joint case for binary and multinomial logit by additionally conditioning on covariates being equal across certain periods. This leads to an estimator whose rate of convergence is slower than n\sqrt{n}. Kyriazidou (2001) combined conditional likelihood with kernel smoothing in dynamic panel sample selection models. Khan, Ouyang and Tamer (2021) generalized Honoré and Kyriazidou (2000) to semiparametric multinomial response models that drop the logit assumption and relax the independence of irrelevant alternatives, establishing point identification but again at a rate slower than n\sqrt{n} that deteriorates with the number of alternatives.

Since there are relatively few models for which sufficient statistics can be found, an alternative approach is to try to construct moment conditions that depend on the common parameters, but not on the individual-specific fixed effects. In the linear case this is what Arellano and Bond (1991) do, when they eliminate the fixed effects by first-differencing and instrument with lagged levels. Papers by Honoré (1993) and Hu (2002) are specific examples of this for panel Tobit models, where the conditions are obtained from a symmetry that is restored through trimming, and the argument is tailored to the censored-regression structure rather than being generic. For multiplicative models, Chamberlain (1992) and Wooldridge (1997) derived moment conditions which are valid without strict exogeneity, implying that lagged dependent variables can be accommodated in count and other nonnegative outcome models. Bonhomme (2012) developed a general approach for obtaining moment conditions via functional differencing, which essentially differences out the unknown distribution of the individual effects in the likelihood. While general, this characterization does not by itself deliver explicit moment functions, and concrete constructions have so far proceeded model by model, exploiting the specific structure of each likelihood. Functional differencing has been operationalized for the dynamic binary logit model by Kitazawa (2022) and Honoré and Weidner (2025), extended to the dynamic ordered logit by Honoré, Muris and Weidner (2025), and given a general transition-probability treatment by Dano (2023). The present paper extends this program to the dynamic multinomial logit.33 3 Al-Sadoon, Li, Pesaran, Yang and Zhao (2026) also consider moment conditions in a dynamic multinomial fixed effects model, but their model is outside the multinomial logit framework and it places restrictions on the support of the fixed effects that depend on the explanatory variables and the model parameters.

Multinomial outcomes are common in applied work with panel data. They arise in choices among employment states (Keane and Wolpin, 1997), consumer products with repeat purchasing and switching costs (Handel, 2013; Dubé, Hitsch and Rossi, 2010), health insurance plans (Pakes, Porter, Shepard and Calder-Wang, 2021), urban consumption locations (Davis, Dingel, Monras and Morales, 2019), and migration destinations (Blumenstock, Chi and Tan, 2025). All of these fit naturally into the multinomial framework. Because switching costs and habit formation are prominent in such settings, it is important to allow lagged choices to enter as regressors and to control for permanent unobserved heterogeneity at the same time (Heckman, 1981).

The construction of our moment conditions is based on a transformed model in which the outcome generated in each period is reassigned according to a permutation σ\sigma of the time indices. For any σ\sigma, the ratio of the transformed-model probability to the true-model probability does not depend on the fixed effects. This follows from the logistic structure, in which the fixed effects enter the choice probabilities via alternative-specific constants whose total contribution depends on the unordered collection of outcomes only — implying invariance to reshuffling outcomes across time. Intuitively, reshuffling outcomes across time leaves the total contribution of the individual effects unchanged, so they can be differenced out through likelihood ratios. When σ\sigma is a cyclic permutation the transformed model is a proper probability distribution, and comparing two such models yields moment conditions of the form required for fixed effects-free estimation; the binary logit conditions of Honoré and Weidner (2025) emerge as the special case with two alternatives. The construction is not specific to the multinomial logit. All that is needed is that the static version of the model admits a sufficient statistic for the fixed effects that is symmetric in the time indices, i.e. a statistic that depends on the outcomes only through their unordered collection. This unifies our results with analogous ones for other models and shows that the approach applies to any dynamic panel model built on a static model that admits conditional likelihood estimation via a symmetric sufficient statistic.

The number of linearly independent moment conditions for given (Q,T)(Q,T) grows rapidly in both the number of alternatives QQ and the number of time periods TT, and we conjecture an explicit formula for this count. We prove that this formula is correct for Q=2Q=2, and that it is a lower bound for T=3T=3 and any QQ. For the other combinations of (Q,T)(Q,T) that we report we verify it numerically. At least three time periods after the initial condition are required, as in the binary case. We give sufficient conditions under which these moments identify the common parameters, the regression and state-dependence coefficients, and propose a generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator. Because the number of available moments grows quickly, only a small subset is typically used in estimation. An empirical application to household soft drink purchases illustrates the importance of controlling for unobserved heterogeneity when estimating state dependence in multinomial choice.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the model. Section 3 presents the moment conditions and establishes their validity. Section 4 generalizes the construction to other dynamic models whose static versions admit a symmetric sufficient statistic for the fixed effects. Section 5 analyzes identification. Section 6 contains the empirical application. Section 7 concludes.

2 Multinomial logit model

Panel settings in which agents repeatedly select from a finite set of alternatives motivate our framework. Examples of such alternatives are brands of a consumer good, transportation modes, employment states, or health insurance plans. Our analysis focuses on two features of these settings: agents differ in their persistent preferences over alternatives (a variation not observed by the econometrician), and past choices can influence current utility (which gives rise to state dependence). Both features produce persistence in the observed choices, so distinguishing them is difficult on the basis of cross-sectional data alone. This is why we use panel data where the same agents are observed over multiple time periods.

We consider panel data with cross-sectional units i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n and time periods t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T. For each pair (i,t)(i,t), we observe the discrete outcome Yi​t∈{1,2,…,Q}Y_{it}\in\{1,2,\ldots,Q\}, where Q∈{2,3,4,…}Q\in\{2,3,4,\ldots\} denotes the number of options. We also observe strictly exogenous regressors Xi​t∈ℝKX_{it}\in\mathbb{R}^{K} for t≥1t\geq 1. The observed outcome at t=0t=0 serves as the initial condition and is conditioned on throughout. For t≥1t\geq 1, the outcomes are generated by the model

Yi​t=argmaxq∈{1,2,…,Q}Uq​i​t,\displaystyle Y_{it}=\operatorname*{argmax}_{q\in\left\{1,2,\ldots,Q\right\}}U_{qit}, (1)

with latent utilities

Uq​i​t\displaystyle U_{qit} =zt​(q,Yi,t−1,Xi,θ)+Aq​i+εq​i​t.\displaystyle=z_{t}(q,Y_{i,t-1},X_{i},\theta)+A_{qi}+\varepsilon_{qit}. (2)

Here, Ai=(A1​i,…,AQ​i)A_{i}=(A_{1i},\ldots,A_{Qi}) are individual-specific fixed effects, and Xi=(Xi​1,Xi​2,…,Xi​T)X_{i}=(X_{i1},X_{i2},\ldots,X_{iT}) are all the strictly exogenous covariates observed for unit ii. The errors εq​i​t\varepsilon_{qit} are independent of (Yi​0,Xi,Ai)(Y_{i0},X_{i},A_{i}), and are assumed to be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) over tt and qq with a type I extreme value distribution.

The vector AiA_{i} collects alternative-specific constants for unit ii, with Aq​iA_{qi} capturing the taste for option qq. Since only differences between the Aq​iA_{qi} enter the choice probabilities, one can normalize A1​i=0A_{1i}=0. The type I extreme value assumption implies that the choice probabilities in (5) below take the form of the familiar multinomial logit model. The independence of irrelevant alternatives across alternatives within each period is therefore the key substantive restriction. Conditioning on Yi​0Y_{i0} throughout avoids the need to specify a model for the initial outcome. This is convenient, because Yi​0Y_{i0} is typically correlated with the fixed effects in an unknown way.

The parameter θ\theta is unknown, but the function zt​(⋅,⋅,⋅,θ)z_{t}(\cdot,\cdot,\cdot,\theta) is known up to θ\theta. The standard linear specification reads

zt(q,Yi,t−1,Xi,θ)=∑r=1Qγq​r 1{Yi,t−1=r}+Xi​t′βq,\displaystyle z_{t}(q,Y_{i,t-1},X_{i},\theta)=\sum_{r=1}^{Q}\,\gamma_{qr}\,\mathbbm{1}\left\{Y_{i,t-1}=r\right\}+X_{it}^{\prime}\,\beta_{q}, (3)

with θ=(γ,β)\theta=(\gamma,\beta). Our primary interest is in the state dependence coefficients γq​r\gamma_{qr} and the regression coefficients βq\beta_{q}. The diagonal entries γq​q\gamma_{qq} measure how much the utility of alternative qq rises when qq was also chosen in the previous period. In other words, γq​q\gamma_{qq} captures the degree of habit formation or switching costs for option qq. The off-diagonal entries γq​r\gamma_{qr} with r≠qr\neq q capture additional forms of persistence, including asymmetries between related alternatives. The central difficulty in estimating the persistence coefficients is that one would like to separate genuine state dependence (in the form of the γ\gamma’s) from spurious persistence induced by unobserved heterogeneity. See, for example, Heckman (1981). We address this problem by constructing moment conditions that are free of AiA_{i} but informative about the γ\gamma’s.

The coefficients in the model above are identified only up to normalizations. Three types of shifts leave the choice probabilities unchanged: (i) shifting γq​r\gamma_{qr} by a constant that depends on rr but not on qq, because such a shift appears in the numerator and in every term of the denominator of the logit and therefore cancels; (ii) shifting γq​r\gamma_{qr} by a constant that depends on qq but not on rr, because ∑r=1Q𝟙{Yi,t−1=r}=1\sum_{r=1}^{Q}\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{i,t-1}=r\}=1 and such a shift is therefore equivalent to adding a constant to the utility of alternative qq, which is absorbed into the fixed effect Aq​iA_{qi}; and (iii) shifting βq\beta_{q} by an additive vector in ℝK\mathbb{R}^{K} that does not depend on qq, which cancels between the numerator and denominator of the logit. To remove these sources of non-identification we impose the normalizations γ1​r=0\gamma_{1r}=0 for all r∈{1,…,Q}r\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}, γq​1=0\gamma_{q1}=0 for all q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}, and β1=0\beta_{1}=0. The first of these takes alternative 11 as the reference alternative, as in Magnac (2000), and together with A1​i=0A_{1i}=0 handles the non-identification of type (i). The second takes lagged outcome 11 as the reference lagged state and handles the non-identification of type (ii). The third normalization handles type (iii).

We discuss this model further in Sections 5 and 6.

Let Yi=(Yi​1,Yi​2,…,Yi​T)Y_{i}=(Y_{i1},Y_{i2},\ldots,Y_{iT}). We assume cross-sectional sampling, that is, (Yi,Yi,0,Xi,Ai)(Y_{i},Y_{i,0},X_{i},A_{i}) are i.i.d. distributed across ii. Our goal is to estimate the common parameters θ0\theta_{0} from the observed data as n→∞n\rightarrow\infty with TT fixed. The individual-specific fixed effects AiA_{i} are treated as nuisance parameters. Their distribution is left unspecified, and they are allowed to be arbitrarily correlated with the regressors XiX_{i} and the initial conditions Yi​0Y_{i0}. In this setting, treating the individual-specific fixed effects, AiA_{i}, as parameters to be estimated will lead to the incidental parameter problem (Neyman and Scott, 1948).

3 Moment conditions free of fixed effects

3.1 Moment condition approach

A classic approach to the incidental parameter problem in parametric models is to look for sufficient statistics for the fixed effects. Conditional on these sufficient statistics, the likelihood does not depend on the fixed effects and can be used for estimation. This approach was pioneered by Rasch (1960) and Andersen (1970). For the static multinomial logit model without regressors, Chamberlain (1980) showed that the vector of choice frequencies serves as a sufficient statistic. For dynamic models, Magnac (2000) and Aguirregabiria, Gu and Luo (2021) have developed sufficient statistic approaches. However, these methods do not generally extend to dynamic multinomial logit models with strictly exogenous regressors.

An alternative approach is to construct moment conditions that depend on the common parameters but not on the individual-specific fixed effects. Bonhomme (2012) developed a general framework for obtaining such moment conditions via “functional differencing.” This approach has been applied to dynamic binary logit models by Kitazawa (2022) and Honoré and Weidner (2025), and to dynamic ordered logit models by Honoré, Muris and Weidner (2025). Dano (2023) provides a general treatment using transition probabilities. The present paper extends this approach to the dynamic multinomial logit model.

Formally, we seek moment functions my0​(y,x,θ)∈ℝm_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)\in\mathbb{R} such that

𝔼[mY0(Y,X,θ0)|Y0,X,A]=0\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[m_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\,\Big|\,Y_{0},X,A\right]=0 (8)

for all possible values of the fixed effect AA. Conditioning on the entire covariate path XX here uses the strict exogeneity assumption from Section 2, which rules out feedback from past outcomes to future covariates. For given values of Y0=y0Y_{0}=y_{0}, X=xX=x, θ\theta, and A=αA=\alpha, the distribution of Y=(Y1,…,YT)∈{1,…,Q}TY=(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T})\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T} is given by (7). The conditional moment condition (8) can therefore be written as

∑y∈{1,…,Q}Tmy0​(y,x,θ)​p​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=0,for all ​α∈ℝQ.\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T}}m_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)\,p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=0,\qquad\text{for all }\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{Q}. (9)

This is a system of linear equations in the QTQ^{T} unknowns my0​(y,x,θ)m_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta), where yy ranges over {1,…,Q}T\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T}. The system must hold for all values of α\alpha, which imposes infinitely many constraints. The existence of solutions to this infinite-dimensional system is not guaranteed for arbitrary models, and the distributional assumption on the errors is important for finding valid moment conditions. This linear-algebra view of the problem is the starting point of the functional differencing approach of Bonhomme (2012): valid moment functions are those that lie in the joint null space of the constraints generated by all α∈ℝQ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{Q}.

If we can establish the conditional moment condition (8), then by the law of iterated expectations, we also have the unconditional moment conditions

𝔼⁡[h⁡(Y0,X,θ0)​mY0​(Y,X,θ0)]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[h(Y_{0},X,\theta_{0})\,m_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\right] =0\displaystyle=0 (10)

for any function hh such that the expectation is well-defined. Subject to regularity conditions, these unconditional moment conditions can then be used to estimate the model parameters θ0\theta_{0} by the generalized method of moments (GMM). This approach solves the incidental parameter problem (Neyman and Scott, 1948), because the moment condition (10) does not feature the individual-specific effects AA at all. No assumptions are imposed on the distribution of those nuisance parameters, and they need not be estimated.

Finding a non-trivial solution my0​(y,x,θ)m_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta) to the system (9) is generally hard. The system must hold for all α∈ℝQ\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{Q}, which imposes infinitely many restrictions on the QTQ^{T} unknowns. For arbitrary parametric models, only the trivial solution my0≡0m_{y_{0}}\equiv 0 may exist. Even when non-trivial solutions do exist, they are typically not available in closed form. Bonhomme (2012) provides an abstract characterization of the space of valid moment conditions through functional differencing, but this characterization does not by itself deliver explicit moment functions that can be used for estimation. As a result, explicit constructions of moment functions free of the fixed effects have so far been carried out on a model-by-model basis, relying on features specific to each setting, such as the logit structure in the binary and ordered choice models. The main contribution of this paper is to provide a similar explicit construction for the dynamic multinomial logit model, using the transformed model approach developed in the next subsection.

3.2 Transformed model

Our construction of valid moment functions is based on the concept of a transformed model. The key observation is that the fixed effects AA enter the model probabilities in a specific way, and by comparing the true model with a suitably constructed transformed model, one can eliminate the dependence on AA.

The intuition behind this construction is as follows. The fixed effects AA enter the joint probability p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha) in two ways: (i) through the product ∏t=1Texp⁡(αyt)\prod_{t=1}^{T}\exp(\alpha_{y_t}) in the numerators of the period-by-period choice probabilities, and (ii) through their denominators ∏t=1T∑r=1Qexp⁡(zt​(r,yt−1,x,θ)+αr)\prod_{t=1}^{T}\sum_{r=1}^{Q}\exp\left(z_{t}(r,y_{t-1},x,\theta)+\alpha_{r}\right). Crucially, the numerator product depends on the outcome sequence only through the unordered multiset {y1,…,yT}\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}\}, which renders it invariant under any permutation σ\sigma of the time indices. This implies that comparing the true model with a transformed one that reshuffles outcomes while preserving the denominators will eliminate the fixed effect contribution. We will show below that the resulting likelihood ratio pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)/p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)/p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha) is indeed free of α\alpha (Lemma 2), and that when σ\sigma is a cyclic permutation this ratio can be turned into valid moment conditions for estimation.

Let σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} be a permutation of the time indices. We define the transformed model probability as

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α):=p1​(yσ⁡(T)∣y0,x,θ,α)​∏t=2Tpt​(yσ⁡(t−1)∣yt−1,x,θ,α).\displaystyle p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha):=p_{1}(y_{\sigma(T)}\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)\,\prod_{t=2}^{T}\,p_{t}(y_{\sigma(t-1)}\mid y_{t-1},x,\theta,\alpha). (11)

Compared to the true model, where period tt generates outcome yty_{t}, the transformed model reassigns which outcome is generated in each period: period 1 generates yσ⁡(T)y_{\sigma(T)}, and period t≥2t\geq 2 generates yσ⁡(t−1)y_{\sigma(t-1)}. The true model is the special case σ=σ+\sigma=\sigma_{+}, where σ+\sigma_{+} is the cyclic increment σ+​(t)=t+1\sigma_{+}(t)=t+1 for t<Tt<T and σ+​(T)=1\sigma_{+}(T)=1.

The expression pσp^{\sigma} in (11) is nonnegative by construction, but it does not sum to one over all y∈{1,…,Q}Ty\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T} for arbitrary permutations σ\sigma. For a general permutation σ\sigma, the factors in (11) do not necessarily generate a single cyclic TT-step Markov chain through all TT outcomes. To see this formally, define

τ(k):=σk(T),k=1,…,T,\tau(k):=\sigma^{k}(T),\qquad k=1,\ldots,T, (12)

where σk\sigma^{k} is the kk-fold composition of σ\sigma, e.g. σ2​(T)=σ⁡(σ⁡(T))\sigma^{2}(T)=\sigma(\sigma(T)). The transformed model has a proper Markov structure only if τ\tau visits each index in {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\} exactly once. In this case, τ\tau is itself a permutation of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\}, and pσp^{\sigma} can be rewritten as

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=p1​(yτ⁡(1)∣y0,x,θ,α)​∏k=2Tpτ⁡(k−1)+1​(yτ⁡(k)∣yτ⁡(k−1),x,θ,α).\displaystyle p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=p_{1}(y_{\tau(1)}\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)\prod_{k=2}^{T}p_{\tau(k-1)+1}(y_{\tau(k)}\mid y_{\tau(k-1)},x,\theta,\alpha). (13)

We call the sequence τ=(τ⁡(1),τ⁡(2),…,τ⁡(T))\tau=(\tau(1),\tau(2),\ldots,\tau(T)) the generation order of σ\sigma. The name reflects the role that τ\tau plays in the representation (13): starting from y0y_{0}, the transformed model generates yτ⁡(1)y_{\tau(1)} first, then yτ⁡(2)y_{\tau(2)}, and so on, with yτ⁡(T)y_{\tau(T)} generated last. In other words, the generation order of σ\sigma is the order in which the outcomes y1,…,yTy_{1},\ldots,y_{T} are produced by the transformed model pσp^{\sigma} as a Markov chain. It turns out that (11) can be rewritten as (13) if and only if σ\sigma is a cyclic permutation of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\}. This is a well-known concept in combinatorics, which simply means that T,σ⁡(T),σ2​(T),σ3​(T),…,σT−1​(T)T,\sigma(T),\sigma^{2}(T),\sigma^{3}(T),\ldots,\sigma^{T-1}(T) are all distinct.66 6 Formally, a permutation σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} is cyclic if and only if the orbit of TT under σ\sigma has length TT. Equivalently, {σk(T):k=0,1,…,T−1}={1,…,T}.\{\sigma^{k}(T):k=0,1,\ldots,T-1\}=\{1,\ldots,T\}.

To see why cyclic permutations are the relevant class, recall that every permutation σ\sigma of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\} decomposes into disjoint cycles, and that the sequence τ​(k)=σk​(T)\tau(k)=\sigma^{k}(T) traces only the cycle of σ\sigma containing TT. The reformulation (13) represents the transformed model as a single Markov chain through all TT time periods, which is possible only when the cycle of TT has length TT, that is, when σ\sigma is cyclic. For a non-cyclic σ\sigma, the cycle of TT has length strictly less than TT, and τ⁡(k)\tau(k) returns to TT before visiting the time indices in the other cycles of σ\sigma. In this case pσp^{\sigma} factors as a product of independent Markov chains, one per cycle of σ\sigma. The chains associated with cycles not containing TT are “closed loops” that start and end at the same outcome, and for generic (x,θ,α)(x,\theta,\alpha) they do not sum to one over the corresponding outcomes. The cyclic case is therefore the only one for which ∑ypσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=1\sum_{y}p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=1 holds for all (x,θ,α)(x,\theta,\alpha); see Appendix B for the factorization in the non-cyclic case.

Once we have the reformulation (13), then it is straightforward to show that pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha) sums to one, as summarized by the following lemma.

Lemma 1

If σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} is a cyclic permutation, then

∑y∈{1,…,Q}Tpσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=1.\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T}}p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=1. (14)

Proof of Lemma 1. Since σ\sigma is cyclic, the sequence τ​(k)=σk​(T)\tau(k)=\sigma^{k}(T) visits each index in {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\} exactly once. Hence (11) is a TT-step Markov chain written in a different time order, see (13). Therefore iterated summation gives (14) since at each step ∑j=1Qpt(j∣⋅)=1\sum_{j=1}^{Q}p_{t}(j\mid\cdot)=1.  

3.3 Moment construction

Let σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} be a permutation. Define σ⁡(0):=σ⁡(T)\sigma(0):=\sigma(T). Then (11) can be written more concisely as

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=∏t=1Tpt​(yσ⁡(t−1)∣yt−1,x,θ,α),\displaystyle p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}p_{t}\!\left(y_{\sigma(t-1)}\mid y_{t-1},x,\theta,\alpha\right), (15)

and this definition of σ⁡(0)\sigma(0) will simplify many expressions below.

The ratio of the transformed model probability to the true model probability plays a central role in our construction. The following lemma shows that the ratio pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)/p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)/{p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)} is free of α\alpha and equal to

Sy0σ​(y,x,θ):=exp⁡(∑t=1T[zt​(yσ⁡(t−1),yt−1,x,θ)−zt​(yt,yt−1,x,θ)]).\displaystyle S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta):=\exp\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big[z_{t}\!\left(y_{\sigma(t-1)},y_{t-1},x,\theta\right)-z_{t}\!\left(y_{t},y_{t-1},x,\theta\right)\Big]\right). (16)
Lemma 2

For any permutation σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} we have

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=Sy0σ​(y,x,θ),\displaystyle\frac{p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}{p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}=S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta), (17)

implying that this ratio is free of α\alpha.

Proof of Lemma 2. Using (15) and the definition of the true model,

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=∏t=1Tpt​(yσ⁡(t−1)∣yt−1,x,θ,α)pt​(yt∣yt−1,x,θ,α).\frac{p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}{p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\frac{p_{t}\!\left(y_{\sigma(t-1)}\mid y_{t-1},x,\theta,\alpha\right)}{p_{t}\!\left(y_{t}\mid y_{t-1},x,\theta,\alpha\right)}.

For each tt, the normalizing denominators cancel, so

pt​(yσ⁡(t−1)∣yt−1,x,θ,α)pt​(yt∣yt−1,x,θ,α)=exp⁡(zt​(yσ⁡(t−1),yt−1,x,θ)−zt​(yt,yt−1,x,θ))​exp⁡(αyσ⁡(t−1)−αyt).\frac{p_{t}\!\left(y_{\sigma(t-1)}\mid y_{t-1},x,\theta,\alpha\right)}{p_{t}\!\left(y_{t}\mid y_{t-1},x,\theta,\alpha\right)}=\exp\!\Big(z_{t}(y_{\sigma(t-1)},y_{t-1},x,\theta)-z_{t}(y_{t},y_{t-1},x,\theta)\Big)\,\exp\!\Big(\alpha_{y_{\sigma(t-1)}}-\alpha_{y_{t}}\Big).

Multiplying over tt gives Sy0σ​(y,x,θ)S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta) times

exp⁡(∑t=1Tαyσ⁡(t−1)−∑t=1Tαyt).\exp\!\left(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{y_{\sigma(t-1)}}-\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{y_{t}}\right).

Since σ\sigma is a permutation and σ⁡(0)=σ⁡(T)\sigma(0)=\sigma(T), the indices σ⁡(t−1)\sigma(t-1), t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T, are a reordering of 1,…,T1,\ldots,T. Hence ∑t=1Tαyσ⁡(t−1)=∑t=1Tαyt\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{y_{\sigma(t-1)}}=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\alpha_{y_{t}}, so the α\alpha term cancels. This yields (17).  

Next, let σ\sigma be a cyclic permutation. Then the simplest valid moment condition that follows directly from Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 is

𝔼[1−SY0σ(Y,X,θ0)|Y0,X,A]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[1-S^{\sigma}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\,\Big|\,Y_{0},X,A\right]=0. (18)

To see this, note that

𝔼[SY0σ(Y,X,θ0)∣Y0,X,A]=∑ySY0σ(y,X,θ0)p(y∣Y0,X,θ0,A)=∑ypσ(y∣Y0,X,θ0,A)=1,\mathbb{E}\!\left[S^{\sigma}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\mid Y_{0},X,A\right]=\sum_{y}S^{\sigma}_{Y_{0}}(y,X,\theta_{0})\,p(y\mid Y_{0},X,\theta_{0},A)=\sum_{y}p^{\sigma}(y\mid Y_{0},X,\theta_{0},A)=1,

where the second equality uses (17) and the last equality uses (14).

While valid, the moment function 1−Sy0σ​(y,x,θ)1-S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta) may not be the most useful in practice, because it typically has θ=0\theta=0 as a root regardless of the true parameter value. Indeed, for the linear specification (3) we have zt​(⋅,⋅,x,0)=0z_{t}(\cdot,\cdot,x,0)=0, so Sy0σ​(y,x,0)=1S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,0)=1 for every permutation and every outcome sequence, and the moment function 1−Sσ1-S^{\sigma} vanishes identically at θ=0\theta=0. Moment conditions based on (18) alone therefore cannot separate the true parameter value from zero. The following theorem therefore presents more general valid moment functions.

The construction works by pairing two cyclic permutations σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} whose generation orders τ1\tau_{1} and τ2\tau_{2} agree on their first k−1k-1 entries, but differ at position kk. For both of the transformed models, the first k−1k-1 outcomes Yτ1​(1),…,Yτ1​(k−1)Y_{\tau_{1}(1)},\ldots,Y_{\tau_{1}(k-1)} are produced by identical Markov transitions, so conditioning on these outcomes removes the shared history. The divergence in position kk is what makes the moment function nontrivial. The outcomes in the remaining positions k+1,…,Tk+1,\ldots,T telescope out of the expectation through the Markov factorization (13), leaving an exact cancellation between the two SσS^{\sigma} terms.

Theorem 1

Let σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} be two cyclic permutations of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\}, and define τ1​(k):=σ1k​(T)\tau_{1}(k):=\sigma_{1}^{k}(T) and τ2​(k):=σ2k​(T)\tau_{2}(k):=\sigma_{2}^{k}(T) for k∈{1,…,T}k\in\{1,\ldots,T\}, analogous to (12). Assume σ1≠σ2\sigma_{1}\neq\sigma_{2} and let k∈{1,…,T}k\in\{1,\ldots,T\} be the smallest integer such that τ1​(k)≠τ2​(k)\tau_{1}(k)\neq\tau_{2}(k). Then for any q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}, the moment function

my0σ1,σ2,q(y,x,θ):=𝟙{yτ1​(k)=q}Sy0σ1(y,x,θ)−𝟙{yτ2​(k)=q}Sy0σ2(y,x,θ)\displaystyle m^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},q}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta):=\mathbbm{1}\{y_{\tau_{1}(k)}=q\}\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)-\mathbbm{1}\{y_{\tau_{2}(k)}=q\}\,S^{\sigma_{2}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta) (19)

satisfies

𝔼[mY0σ1,σ2,q(Y,X,θ0)|Yτ1​(1),Yτ1​(2),…,Yτ1​(k−1),Y0,X,A]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[m^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},q}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\,\Big|\,Y_{\tau_{1}(1)},Y_{\tau_{1}(2)},\ldots,Y_{\tau_{1}(k-1)},Y_{0},X,A\right]=0. (20)

This implies that for any function g:{1,…,Q}k−1→ℝg:\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{k-1}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} we have

𝔼[g(Yτ1​(1),Yτ1​(2),…,Yτ1​(k−1))mY0σ1,σ2,q(Y,X,θ0)|Y0,X,A]=0.\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[g(Y_{\tau_{1}(1)},Y_{\tau_{1}(2)},\ldots,Y_{\tau_{1}(k-1)})\;m^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},q}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\,\Big|\,Y_{0},X,A\right]=0. (21)

Proof of Theorem 1. It suffices to prove (20), since (21) follows by multiplying by g⁡(Yτ1​(1),…,Yτ1​(k−1))g(Y_{\tau_{1}(1)},\ldots,Y_{\tau_{1}(k-1)}) and taking iterated expectations.

Fix arbitrary q1,…,qk−1∈{1,…,Q}q_{1},\ldots,q_{k-1}\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}. For i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, Lemma 2 gives Sσi=pσi/pS^{\sigma_{i}}=p^{\sigma_{i}}/p, so

𝔼[𝟙{Yτi​(k)=q}SY0σi(Y,X,θ0)⋅∏j=1k−1𝟙{Yτ1​(j)=qj}|Y0,X,A]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{\tau_{i}(k)}=q\}\,S^{\sigma_{i}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\cdot\prod_{j=1}^{k-1}\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{\tau_{1}(j)}=q_{j}\}\,\Big|\,Y_{0},X,A\right]
=∑y∈{1,…,Q}T:yτ1​(j)=qj​∀j=1,…,k−1𝟙{yτi​(k)=q}pσi(y∣Y0,X,θ0,A).\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}y\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T}:\\ y_{\tau_{1}(j)}=q_{j}\ \forall\,j=1,\ldots,k-1\end{subarray}}\mathbbm{1}\{y_{\tau_{i}(k)}=q\}\;p^{\sigma_{i}}(y\mid Y_{0},X,\theta_{0},A).

By the Markov factorization (13), summing over the remaining components yτi​(k+1),…,yτi​(T)y_{\tau_{i}(k+1)},\ldots,y_{\tau_{i}(T)} telescopes to one, and the right-hand side equals

p1​(q1∣Y0,X,θ0,A)​∏j=2k−1pτi​(j−1)+1​(qj∣qj−1,X,θ0,A)⋅pτi​(k−1)+1​(q∣qk−1,X,θ0,A).p_{1}(q_{1}\mid Y_{0},X,\theta_{0},A)\,\prod_{j=2}^{k-1}p_{\tau_{i}(j-1)+1}(q_{j}\mid q_{j-1},X,\theta_{0},A)\,\cdot\,p_{\tau_{i}(k-1)+1}(q\mid q_{k-1},X,\theta_{0},A).

For k=1k=1 no outcomes are held fixed, and the right-hand side is simply p1​(q∣Y0,X,θ0,A)p_{1}(q\mid Y_{0},X,\theta_{0},A). Since τ1​(j)=τ2​(j)\tau_{1}(j)=\tau_{2}(j) for all j≤k−1j\leq k-1, this expression is the same for i=1i=1 and i=2i=2. Hence the two terms in (19) cancel. Since this holds for all (q1,…,qk−1)(q_{1},\ldots,q_{k-1}), equation (20) follows.  

3.3.1 Example: moment conditions for T=3T=3

To illustrate, consider T=3T=3. There are (T−1)!=2(T-1)!=2 cyclic permutations of {1,2,3}\{1,2,3\}: the cyclic increment σ+\sigma_{+}, which gives the true model, and the reverse cycle σ1\sigma_{1} defined by σ1​(1)=3\sigma_{1}(1)=3, σ1​(2)=1\sigma_{1}(2)=1, σ1​(3)=2\sigma_{1}(3)=2. Taking σ2=σ+\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{+}, the generation orders are τ1=(2,1,3)\tau_{1}=(2,1,3) and τ2=(1,2,3)\tau_{2}=(1,2,3), which first differ at k=1k=1. Since σ2=σ+\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{+} is the true model, Sy0σ2​(y,x,θ)=1S^{\sigma_{2}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)=1, and Theorem 1 yields QQ conditional moment conditions:

𝔼[𝟙{Y2=q}SY0σ1(Y,X,θ0)−𝟙{Y1=q}|Y0,X,A]=0,q=1,…,Q,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\Big[\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{2}=q\}\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})-\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{1}=q\}\,\Big|\,Y_{0},X,A\Big]=0,\quad q=1,\ldots,Q, (22)

where, by (16),

Sy0σ1​(y,x,θ)=exp⁡(CLOSE\displaystyle S^{\sigma_{1}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)=\exp\!\Big( z1​(y2,y0,x,θ)−z1​(y1,y0,x,θ)\displaystyle z_{1}(y_{2},y_{0},x,\theta)-z_{1}(y_{1},y_{0},x,\theta)
+z2​(y3,y1,x,θ)−z2​(y2,y1,x,θ)\displaystyle+z_{2}(y_{3},y_{1},x,\theta)-z_{2}(y_{2},y_{1},x,\theta)
OPEN+z3​(y1,y2,x,θ)−z3​(y3,y2,x,θ)).\displaystyle+z_{3}(y_{1},y_{2},x,\theta)-z_{3}(y_{3},y_{2},x,\theta)\Big). (23)

For Q=2Q=2, the moment conditions (22) recover the leading result for the dynamic binary logit model with T=3T=3 in Honoré and Weidner (2025). The transformed model approach provides a particularly transparent derivation of these known moment conditions for Q=2Q=2.

More generally, varying (σ1,σ2,q,g)(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},q,g) over all admissible choices in Theorem 1 generates a large family of valid moment functions, many of which are linearly dependent. Determining the number of linearly independent moment conditions that this construction yields, as a function of QQ and TT, is the subject of the next subsection.

3.4 Counting of linearly independent moment conditions

Theorem 1 produces a large family of moment functions as we vary the cyclic permutations σ1,σ2\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2} and the weighting function gg. Many choices will generate moment conditions that are redundant, in the sense that they can be written as linear combinations of others in the family. It is therefore useful to know how many linearly independent moment conditions can be obtained from the theorem.

We now describe an explicit parameterization that extracts ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) moment functions from Theorem 1, where ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) is the count given in (25) below. The moment functions will be indexed by tuples (j,𝐭,s2,𝐪)(j,\mathbf{t},s_{2},\mathbf{q}) where j∈{0,1,…,T−3}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,T-3\} is an integer that records the number of shared time indices between the two generation orders of Theorem 1, 𝐭=(t1<⋯<tj)\mathbf{t}=(t_{1}<\cdots<t_{j}) is a collection of jj time periods in {1,…,T−1}\{1,\ldots,T-1\}, s1:=min⁡({1,…,T−1}∖𝐭)s_{1}:=\min(\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\setminus\mathbf{t}) is therefore determined by 𝐭\mathbf{t}, and s2s_{2} is any element of {1,…,T−1}∖(𝐭∪{s1})\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\setminus(\mathbf{t}\cup\{s_{1}\}), and 𝐪=(q0,q1,…,qj)∈{1,…,Q}j+1\mathbf{q}=(q_{0},q_{1},\ldots,q_{j})\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{j+1} is a vector of outcome values. For each such tuple the corresponding moment function takes the form

my0j,𝐭,s1,s2,𝐪(y,x,θ):=[∏l=1j{ytl=ql}][𝟙{ys1=q0}Sy0σ1(y,x,θ)−𝟙{ys2=q0}Sy0σ2(y,x,θ)],\displaystyle m^{j,\mathbf{t},s_{1},s_{2},\mathbf{q}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)\;:=\;\left[\prod_{l=1}^{j}\mathbbm{1}\!\left\{y_{t_{l}}=q_{l}\right\}\right]\Big[\mathbbm{1}\{y_{s_{1}}=q_{0}\}\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)-\mathbbm{1}\{y_{s_{2}}=q_{0}\}\,S^{\sigma_{2}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)\Big], (24)

where σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} are the two cyclic permutations of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\} whose generation orders agree on the first jj entries (t1,…,tj)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{j}) but differ at position j+1j+1, with σ1\sigma_{1} placing s1s_{1} at that position and σ2\sigma_{2} placing s2s_{2}.77 7 Explicitly, σ1\sigma_{1} has generation order τ1=(t1,…,tj,s1,r1,…,rT−j−3,s2,T)\tau_{1}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{j},s_{1},r_{1},\ldots,r_{T-j-3},s_{2},T) and σ2\sigma_{2} has generation order τ2=(t1,…,tj,s2,r1,…,rT−j−3,s1,T)\tau_{2}=(t_{1},\ldots,t_{j},s_{2},r_{1},\ldots,r_{T-j-3},s_{1},T), where r1<⋯<rT−j−3r_{1}<\cdots<r_{T-j-3} are the remaining elements of {1,…,T−1}∖(𝐭∪{s1,s2})\{1,\ldots,T-1\}\setminus(\mathbf{t}\cup\{s_{1},s_{2}\}) in increasing order. Since the generation orders first differ at position k=j+1k=j+1, Theorem 1 applies with this kk, q=q0q=q_{0}, and weighting function g(yt1,…,ytj)=∏l=1j𝟙{ytl=ql}g(y_{t_{1}},\ldots,y_{t_{j}})=\prod_{l=1}^{j}\mathbbm{1}\{y_{t_{l}}=q_{l}\}, and guarantees that my0j,𝐭,s1,s2,𝐪m^{j,\mathbf{t},s_{1},s_{2},\mathbf{q}}_{y_{0}} satisfies (8) at θ=θ0\theta=\theta_{0}.

To avoid counting redundant moment functions, we further impose the restriction tr=rt_{r}=r for r=1,…,max⁡(0,j−(Q−2))r=1,\ldots,\max(0,j-(Q-2)) on 𝐭\mathbf{t}.88 8 Without this restriction the construction would yield more tuples than ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T), but those additional moment functions would be linearly dependent on those in the constrained set. For j≤Q−2j\leq Q-2 the restriction is vacuous; for j>Q−2j>Q-2 it fixes the first j−(Q−2)j-(Q-2) entries of 𝐭\mathbf{t} to the smallest possible values 1,2,…,j−(Q−2)1,2,\ldots,j-(Q-2).

Counting the distinct tuples (j,𝐭,s2,𝐪)(j,\mathbf{t},s_{2},\mathbf{q}) that satisfy all the restrictions above then gives99 9 For each jj, the restriction on 𝐭\mathbf{t} fixes max⁡(0,j−(Q−2))\max(0,j-(Q-2)) of its entries and leaves min⁡(j,Q−2)\min(j,Q-2) entries to be chosen freely from the T−1−max⁡(0,j−(Q−2))T-1-\max(0,j-(Q-2)) remaining positions in {1,…,T−1}\{1,\ldots,T-1\}, giving (T−1−max⁡(j−(Q−2), 0)min⁡(Q−2,j))\binom{T-1-\max(j-(Q-2),\,0)}{\min(Q-2,\,j)} choices for 𝐭\mathbf{t}. Summing the product of these three counts over j∈{0,1,…,T−3}j\in\{0,1,\ldots,T-3\} yields (25).

ℓ⁡(Q,T)=∑j=0T−3(T−1−max⁡(j−(Q−2), 0)min⁡(Q−2,j))⋅(T−2−j)⋅Qj+1.\displaystyle\ell(Q,T)\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{T-3}\binom{T-1-\max(j-(Q-2),\,0)}{\min(Q-2,\,j)}\cdot(T-2-j)\cdot Q^{j+1}. (25)

For small values of QQ this simplifies to ℓ⁡(2,T)=2T−2​T\ell(2,T)=2^{T}-2T, ℓ⁡(3,T)=3T−(3​T2)+6​(T−1)\ell(3,T)=3^{T}-\binom{3T}{2}+6(T-1), and ℓ⁡(4,T)=4T−(4​T3)+40​(T−1)2\ell(4,T)=4^{T}-\binom{4T}{3}+40(T-1)^{2}. More generally, for Q≥T−1Q\geq T-1, it becomes ℓ⁡(Q,T)=QT−Q⁡(2+Q−T)​(1+Q)T−2\ell(Q,T)=Q^{T}-Q(2+Q-T)(1+Q)^{T-2}. In each case the formula has the structure ℓ⁡(Q,T)=QT−r⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T)=Q^{T}-r(Q,T), where the ambient dimension QTQ^{T} counts all real-valued functions of the outcome sequence yy, and the subtracted term r⁡(Q,T)r(Q,T) counts the linear restrictions on mm imposed by requiring the moment condition (9) to hold for all values of the fixed effect α\alpha.

Numerical investigations and the partial analytical results discussed in Appendix A lead us to the following conjecture.

Conjecture 1

For T≥3T\geq 3 and Q≥2Q\geq 2 and for generic (y0,x,θ0)(y_{0},x,\theta_{0}), the ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) moment functions in (24) are linearly independent, and every valid moment function of the form (8) at θ=θ0\theta=\theta_{0} is a linear combination of them.

The status of the conjecture is as follows. For Q=2Q=2 the lower bound follows from the explicit moment functions of Honoré and Weidner (2025), and the matching upper bound is established in subsequent work; see Dobronyi, Gu, Kim and Russell (2021) and Dano (2023). For T=3T=3 and any Q≥2Q\geq 2, we prove in Appendix A that the ℓ⁡(Q,3)=Q\ell(Q,3)=Q moment functions in (24) are linearly independent, so the dimension of the space of valid moment conditions is at least ℓ⁡(Q,3)\ell(Q,3). For all combinations of (Q,T)(Q,T) reported in Table 1, the conjecture has been verified by direct numerical computation. A general analytical proof of the conjecture remains an open problem. Appendix A discusses two natural proof strategies (a polynomial expansion of the likelihood and a direct linear-independence argument on the moments in (24)) and identifies the technical obstacle.

The qualifier “generic” in the conjecture means that it is expected to hold outside a measure-zero subset of (Y0,X,θ0)(Y_{0},X,\theta_{0}). For special values of XX and θ0\theta_{0}, additional moment conditions may become available, so the total number of linearly independent moment conditions can exceed ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T).

Table 1 reports ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) for combinations relevant for empirical applications. Two features are worth noting. First, ℓ⁡(Q,T)=0\ell(Q,T)=0 for T≤2T\leq 2 for every QQ, which confirms that at least three time periods after the initial condition are required for moment conditions free of the fixed effects to exist for generic parameters. Second, the count grows quickly in both QQ and TT: with Q=4Q=4 alternatives and T=5T=5 time periods, the parameterization yields 524 linearly independent moment conditions for each value of the initial condition. Only a small subset of these moment conditions is typically used for estimation in practice. We return to this issue in Section 6.

4 Moment conditions for more general models

Most of the derivations in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 are generic and do not use the specific structure of the multinomial logit model. The only exception is Lemma 2 which establishes that for any permutation σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,T\},

Sy0σ​(y,x,θ):=pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)S_{y_{0}}^{\sigma}(y,x,\theta):=\frac{p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}{p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)} (26)

is free of α\alpha. In this section, we characterize a larger class of models for which this is true, and it follows that moment conditions can be constructed using the arguments of Sections 3.2 and 3.3 for any model in this larger class.

Consider the model for the joint distribution of (Y1,Y2,…,YT)\left(Y_{1},Y_{2},\ldots,Y_{T}\right):

p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=P⁡(Y=y|Y0=y0,x,A=α)=∏t=1Tf⁡(yt,zt​(yt−1,x,θ),α)p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=P\left(Y=y\,\Big|\,Y_{0}=y_{0},x,A=\alpha\right)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(y_{t},z_{t}\left(y_{t-1},x,\theta\right),\alpha) (27)

for functions ff and z1,…,zTz_{1},\ldots,z_{T}.

Lemma 3

Let pp be defined as in (27). Assume that for every (η1,…,ηT)(\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{T}) in the range of the functions ztz_{t}, the joint distribution

∏t=1Tf⁡(yt,ηt,α)\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(y_{t},\eta_{t},\alpha)

on the outcome space of (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) admits a statistic S=s⁡(Y1,…,YT)S=s(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) such that the conditional distribution of (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) given SS does not depend on α\alpha, and that ss is symmetric in its arguments (so that s⁡(yπ⁡(1),…,yπ⁡(T))=s⁡(y1,…,yT)s(y_{\pi(1)},\ldots,y_{\pi(T)})=s(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}) for every permutation π\pi of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\}). Then for any permutation σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,T\}, the ratio

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=Sy0σ​(y,x,θ)\frac{p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}{p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}=S_{y_{0}}^{\sigma}(y,x,\theta)

is free of α\alpha.

Proof of Lemma 3. The assumptions imply that for any values of η1,…,ηT\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{T}, the ratio ∏t=1Tf⁡(st,ηt,α)∏t=1Tf⁡(yt,ηt,α)\frac{\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(s_{t},\eta_{t},\alpha)}{\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(y_{t},\eta_{t},\alpha)} does not depend on α\alpha provided that (s1,…,sT)\left(s_{1},\ldots,s_{T}\right) is a permutation of (y1,…,yT)\left(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}\right). With ηt=zt​(yt−1,x,θ)\eta_{t}=z_{t}\left(y_{t-1},x,\theta\right), we then have

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=f⁡(yσ⁡(T),η1,α)​∏t=2Tf⁡(yσ⁡(t−1),ηt,α)∏t=1Tf⁡(yt,ηt,α).\frac{p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}{p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)}=\frac{f(y_{\sigma(T)},\eta_{1},\alpha)\,\prod_{t=2}^{T}\,f(y_{\sigma(t-1)},\eta_{t},\alpha)}{\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(y_{t},\eta_{t},\alpha)}.

Since (yσ⁡(T),yσ⁡(1),…,yσ⁡(T−1))\left(y_{\sigma(T)},y_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,y_{\sigma(T-1)}\right) is a permutation of (y1,…,yT)\left(y_{1},\ldots,y_{T}\right), this does not depend on α\alpha.  

Combining Lemma 3 with the results in Sections 3.2 and 3.3 implies that for any static model for which there exists a symmetric sufficient statistic for AA, it is possible to construct moment conditions for the corresponding dynamic model in which Yt−1Y_{t-1} is an explanatory variable in period tt. This unifies some known results and makes it clear how to construct moment conditions in models that have not previously been considered in the literature. Moreover, the logic behind the construction also applies to continuous distributions. We provide some examples below.

4.1 Example: exponential–family panel models (Hahn 1997)

A rich class of models satisfying the hypotheses of Lemma 3 is provided by the exponential–family panel models studied by Hahn (1997). In the notation of (27), the period–tt density takes the form

f⁡(yt,η,α)=exp⁡(s​(yt)′​α​e​(θ)+d⁡(η,α,θ)+b⁡(yt,η,θ)),f(y_{t},\eta,\alpha)=\exp\!\big(\,s(y_{t})^{\prime}\,\alpha\,e(\theta)+d(\eta,\alpha,\theta)+b(y_{t},\eta,\theta)\,\big), (28)

where α\alpha is the fixed effect, η=zt​(yt−1,x,θ)\eta=z_{t}(y_{t-1},x,\theta) is the index, s⁡(⋅)s(\cdot) is a vector of canonical statistics, e⁡(θ)e(\theta) is a known function of the common parameter, d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) is the log–normalizing constant (which does not involve yty_{t}), and b⁡(⋅)b(\cdot) collects the remaining terms, which involve yty_{t} and the index but not the fixed effect. This is the model in equation (1) of Hahn (1997), with the role of the regressors played here by the index η\eta, and as Hahn (1997) notes, this class contains the panel linear regression model with normal errors, the panel logit model, the panel Poisson regression model, and the panel negative binomial model.

Consider the static case where η=zt​(yt−1,x,θ)\eta=z_{t}(y_{t-1},x,\theta) does not depend on yt−1y_{t-1}. In this case,

S⁡(Y)=∑t=1Ts⁡(Yt)S(Y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}s(Y_{t})

is a sufficient statistic for α\alpha, and it is symmetric in (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) (Lemma 4 of Appendix C). The assumptions of Lemma 3 are therefore satisfied, and the moment–condition construction of Sections 3.2–3.3 applies to a model that includes lagged dependent variables as explanatory variables.

To obtain the moment functions explicitly, form the ratio pσ/pp^{\sigma}/p using (28). The normalizing constants d⁡(ηt,α,θ)d(\eta_{t},\alpha,\theta) cancel period by period; and because ∑ts⁡(yσ⁡(t−1))=∑ts⁡(yt)\sum_{t}s(y_{\sigma(t-1)})=\sum_{t}s(y_{t}), the fixed effect term s​(yt)′​α​e​(θ)s(y_{t})^{\prime}\alpha\,e(\theta) cancels as well. What remains is

Sy0σ​(y,x,θ)=exp⁡(∑t=1T[b⁡(yσ⁡(t−1),ηt,θ)−b⁡(yt,ηt,θ)]),ηt=zt​(yt−1,x,θ),S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)=\exp\!\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big[\,b\big(y_{\sigma(t-1)},\eta_{t},\theta\big)-b\big(y_{t},\eta_{t},\theta\big)\,\big]\Big),\qquad\eta_{t}=z_{t}(y_{t-1},x,\theta), (29)

which is free of α\alpha, in agreement with Lemma 3. Exactly as in Theorem 1, take T=3T=3, σ2=σ+\sigma_{2}=\sigma_{+} (so that Sσ2≡1S^{\sigma_{2}}\equiv 1), and σ1\sigma_{1} the reverse cycle; when YY is continuous the indicator 𝟙{Yτ⁡(k)=q}\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{\tau(k)}=q\} is replaced by an arbitrary bounded function gg, and the moment condition is that, for every such gg,

𝔼[g(Y2)SY0σ1(Y,X,θ0)−g(Y1)|Y0,X,A]=0.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,g(Y_{2})\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})-g(Y_{1})\;\Big|\;Y_{0},X,A\,\right]=0. (30)

The validity of (30) is established more formally in Proposition 3 of Appendix C.

4.2 Example: sufficient statistics that depend on θ\theta

The model in (28) implies a sufficient statistic that is free of the common parameter and the regressors. However, the construction of moment conditions suggested above requires only that the static model admits a sufficient statistic for AA that is symmetric in the time indices. It therefore applies more broadly, including cases in which the relevant statistic depends on θ\theta, so long as symmetry across tt is preserved. A bivariate gamma panel model in the spirit of Lindsay (1982) illustrates this. For each tt the outcome is the pair Yt=(Y1​t,Y2​t)Y_{t}=(Y_{1t},Y_{2t}) where, conditional on the past, the regressors, and the fixed effect AA, the two components are independent with1010 10 These use the common shape–rate parameterization.

Y1​t∼Gamma⁡(z1​t,A),Y2​t∼Gamma⁡(z2​t,ϕ​A),Y_{1t}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\!\left(z_{1t},\,A\right),\qquad Y_{2t}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}\!\left(z_{2t},\,\phi A\right), (31)

where zj​t=zj​t​(yt−1,X,θ)z_{jt}=z_{jt}(y_{t-1},X,\theta) for j=1,2j=1,2 and θ=(β1′,β2′,ϕ)′\theta=(\beta_{1}^{\prime},\beta_{2}^{\prime},\phi)^{\prime}. In the static case where the zj​t​(yt−1,X,θ)z_{jt}(y_{t-1},X,\theta) do not depend on yt−1y_{t-1},

sθ​(Y)=∑t=1TY1​t+ϕ​∑t=1TY2​ts_{\theta}(Y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_{1t}+\phi\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_{2t}

is a sufficient statistic for AA in the sense that the distribution of (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) conditional on sθ​(Y)s_{\theta}(Y) does not depend on AA. It is symmetric in the time indices, but in contrast to (28), it depends on the common parameter θ\theta through ϕ\phi, so the model lies outside the class of Hahn (1997). Symmetry is nonetheless all that our moment conditions construction requires, and the same cancellation gives

Sy0σ​(y,X,θ)=exp⁡(∑t=1T[z1​t​(log⁡y1,σ⁡(t−1)−log⁡y1​t)+z2​t​(log⁡y2,σ⁡(t−1)−log⁡y2​t)]),S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,X,\theta)=\exp\!\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big[\,z_{1t}\,(\log y_{1,\sigma(t-1)}-\log y_{1t})+z_{2t}\,(\log y_{2,\sigma(t-1)}-\log y_{2t})\,\big]\Big), (32)

free of AA, so that, for any bounded gg on the outcome space,

𝔼[g(Y2)SY0σ1(Y,X,θ0)−g(Y1)|Y0,X,A]=0;\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,g(Y_{2})\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})-g(Y_{1})\;\Big|\;Y_{0},X,A\,\right]=0; (33)

see Appendix C for details. The cross–equation parameter ϕ\phi enters only through the fixed effect–coupled rate of Y2​tY_{2t} and hence cancels from SσS^{\sigma} together with AA. The construction thus delivers moment conditions for the index parameters (β1,β2)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}), while identifying ϕ\phi would require other arguments.1111 11 For example, ϕ\phi may be recovered as ϕ=𝔼⁡[Y1​tz1​t]/𝔼⁡[Y2​tz2​t]\phi=\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Y_{1t}}{z_{1t}}\right]/\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{Y_{2t}}{z_{2t}}\right] if β1,β2\beta_{1},\beta_{2} are identified. This readily follows from the expression of the mean for a Gamma distribution. Of course in this case, different moment conditions for (β1,β2)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}) could have also been constructed using the marginal distributions for Y1​tY_{1t} and Y2​tY_{2t} and the fact that the fixed effect enters the means of Y1​tY_{1t} and Y2​tY_{2t} multiplicatively.

4.3 Example: linear panel data models with normal errors

The linear panel data model with normal errors and additive fixed effects,

Yt=zt(Yt−1,X,θ)+A+εt,εt∣(Yt−1,X,A)∼𝒩(0,σ2),Y_{t}=z_{t}(Y_{t-1},X,\theta)+A+\varepsilon_{t},\qquad\varepsilon_{t}\mid(Y^{t-1},X,A)\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), (34)

is also a special case of (28), with the fixed effect entering through the canonical statistic s⁡(yt)=yts(y_{t})=y_{t}. Hence S⁡(Y)=∑t=1TYtS(Y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}Y_{t} is a symmetric sufficient statistic for AA, and Lemma 3 applies. In forming pσ/pp^{\sigma}/p, the terms in yt2y_{t}^{2}, which do not involve the index, cancel by symmetry along with the fixed effect, leaving

Sy0σ​(y,x,θ)=exp⁡(1σ2​∑t=1Tzt​(yt−1,x,θ)​(yσ⁡(t−1)−yt)),S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)=\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{\sigma^{2}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}z_{t}(y_{t-1},x,\theta)\,\big(y_{\sigma(t-1)}-y_{t}\big)\Big), (35)

and the moment condition 𝔼[g(Y2)SY0σ1(Y,X,θ0)−g(Y1)∣Y0,X,A]=0\mathbb{E}\big[g(Y_{2})\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})-g(Y_{1})\mid Y_{0},X,A\big]=0 for any bounded gg.

This example is instructive because it exposes the limits of the moment condition construction above. The model (34) already admits an obvious and well–behaved set of fixed effect-free moment conditions: because Yt−zt=A+εtY_{t}-z_{t}=A+\varepsilon_{t}, any contrast that differences out the fixed effect, such as

𝔼[(Yt−zt)−(Yt−1−zt−1)∣Y0,X,A]=0,\mathbb{E}\big[(Y_{t}-z_{t})-(Y_{t-1}-z_{t-1})\mid Y_{0},X,A\big]=0, (36)

is linear in the data, possesses moments of all orders, and is the basis for the standard linear panel data estimators (Arellano and Bond, 1991). When ztz_{t} is linear in the lagged outcome, the moment function (35) produced by our construction is, by contrast, the exponential of a quadratic 1212 12 Interestingly, using a different approach Kitazawa (2001) derived moment conditions for a model like (34) that are based on exponential of linear functions of Gaussian outcomes. form in the Gaussian outcomes — the quadratic arising from the lagged outcome inside ztz_{t} --- and is consequently heavy--tailed. Its conditional variance need not exist: it is finite only when the state--dependence coefficient lies in a bounded interval, and successively smaller intervals are required for the higher moments,1313 13 For example, with zt​(yt−1,x,θ)=γ​yt−1+xt′​βz_{t}(y_{t-1},x,\theta)=\gamma\,y_{t-1}+x_{t}^{\prime}\beta and T=3T=3, the conditional second moment 𝔼[(SY0σ1)2∣Y0,X,A]\mathbb{E}\big[(S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}})^{2}\mid Y_{0},X,A\big] is finite if and only if γ\gamma lies between the two real roots of 1−4​γ2+4​γ3−4​γ41-4\gamma^{2}+4\gamma^{3}-4\gamma^{4}, that is, γ∈(−0.400, 0.575)\gamma\in(-0.400,\,0.575); more generally the kk–th conditional moment is finite if and only if 2​k​(k−1)​γ2​(1−γ+γ2)<12k(k-1)\,\gamma^{2}(1-\gamma+\gamma^{2})<1. and outside these ranges the moment has infinite variance and the associated estimator is no longer n\sqrt{n}–asymptotically normal. Even where the variance is finite, the moment is strongly right–skewed, so generalized method of moments estimators based on it can be very imprecise. We conclude from this example that the transformed–model approach can sometimes best be understood as a device for generating valid fixed effect-free moment conditions when no problem–specific reduction is apparent. The moment functions it delivers are always valid, but, as (35) illustrates, they need not be well behaved, and they may be dominated by simple alternatives such as the differencing moments (36) that a model–specific analysis would suggest. The construction therefore complements, but does not substitute for, case–specific reasoning about how best to eliminate the fixed effects.

5 Identification

In earlier work, Honoré and Kyriazidou (2000) studied the dynamic multinomial logit model with the linear specification (3) and showed that θ0\theta_{0} can be identified with only T=3T=3 periods. The key restriction they require is that the regressors do not vary over the last two periods, X2=X3X_{2}=X_{3}. This makes it possible to construct a conditional likelihood that eliminates the fixed effects and leads to an elegant identification argument.1414 14 It can be shown that under the restriction X2=X3X_{2}=X_{3}, model (7) admits additional valid moment functions beyond those presented in Theorem 1. The score of the conditional likelihood in Honoré and Kyriazidou (2000) involves a particular linear combination of these extra moments. Here, our argument relies only on the moment conditions in Theorem 1, which remain valid without imposing X2=X3X_{2}=X_{3} and can therefore be used for n\sqrt{n}-consistent estimation with continuous covariates.

The drawback is that this restriction is demanding when covariates are continuous, as in our empirical application which features product-specific prices. In that case, the event X2=X3X_{2}=X_{3} has probability zero, so estimation relies only on the few observations for which X2X_{2} and X3X_{3} are close, implying in turn a slower-than-n\sqrt{n} rate of convergence.

This section shows that this shortcoming can be avoided by leveraging the fixed effect free moment condition in Theorem 1. We illustrate this point in the context of our empirical specification (4),

zt(q,Yi,t−1,Xi,θ)=γq𝟙{Yi,t−1=q}+Xi​t,qβ,\displaystyle z_{t}(q,Y_{i,t-1},X_{i},\theta)=\gamma_{q}\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{i,t-1}=q\}+X_{it,q}\beta,

with T=3T=3 periods. The target parameter is θ0=(β0,γ01,…,γ0​Q)∈Θ⊂ℝQ+1\theta_{0}=(\beta_{0},\gamma_{01},\ldots,\gamma_{0Q})\in\Theta\subset\mathbb{R}^{Q+1} and Proposition 1 shows that it is uniquely identified under support conditions that do not require constancy of the covariates across certain periods. We impose the following assumptions.

Assumption 1

(Rectangular Compact Parameter Space). The parameter space is

Θ=[β¯,β¯]×[γ¯,γ¯]Q\displaystyle\Theta=[\underline{\beta},\overline{\beta}]\times[\underline{\gamma},\overline{\gamma}]^{Q}

for scalars β¯<0<β¯\underline{\beta}<0<\overline{\beta}, γ¯<0<γ¯\underline{\gamma}<0<\overline{\gamma}.

Assumption 2

(Identification Restrictions). The outcomes Y=(Y1,Y2,Y3)Y=(Y_{1},Y_{2},Y_{3}) are generated according to model (7) with z.(.,.,.,.)z_{.}(.,.,.,.) defined in (4) for Q≥3Q\geq 3,1515 15 We focus our attention on the case Q≥3Q\geq 3 as Honoré and Weidner (2025) already provided sufficient conditions for identification in the binary case Q=2Q=2. T=3T=3, and true parameter θ0=(β0,γ01,…,γ0​Q)∈Θ\theta_{0}=(\beta_{0},\gamma_{01},\ldots,\gamma_{0Q})\in\Theta. Moreover, for any initial condition y0∈{1,…,Q}y_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}, there exists a non-empty set 𝒳y0r​e​g⊆ℝ3​Q\mathcal{X}_{y_{0}}^{reg}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3Q} and a compact set 𝒜y0r​e​g\mathcal{A}^{reg}_{y_{0}} such that for all x∈𝒳y0r​e​gx\in\mathcal{X}_{y_{0}}^{reg},
P⁡(A∈𝒜y0r​e​g|Y0=y0,X=x)P(A\in\mathcal{A}^{reg}_{y_{0}}|Y_{0}=y_{0},X=x) is well defined and bounded away from zero.

Assumption 1 is standard. Assumption 2 imposes the regularity conditions employed in our identification argument. In particular, it guarantees that, the model probabilities of all choice histories y=(y1,y2,y3)y=(y_{1},y_{2},y_{3}) remain strictly positive for each initial condition y0y_{0}.
Our identification strategy exploits the conditional moment functions in (19). With T=3T=3 periods, they take the form

my0σ1,σ+,q(y,x,θ)≡my0σ1,q(y,x,θ)=𝟙{y2=q}Sy0σ1(y,x,θ)−𝟙{y1=q},\displaystyle m_{y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{+},q}(y,x,\theta)\equiv m_{y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},q}(y,x,\theta)=\mathbbm{1}\big\{y_{2}=q\big\}S^{\sigma_{1}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)-\mathbbm{1}\big\{y_{1}=q\big\}, (37)

where σ+\sigma_{+} is the cyclical increment and σ1\sigma_{1} is the reverse cycle. The core idea behind Proposition 1 is to craft a just-identified system of moment equations Ξ⁡(θ)\Xi(\theta) based on (37) whose Jacobian ∇Ξ​(θ)\nabla\Xi(\theta) forms a PP-matrix on the whole parameter space Θ\Theta; that is, a matrix with all principal minors positive. This property allows us to invoke a global univalence theorem of Gale and Nikaido (1965), which implies that Ξ⁡(θ)\Xi(\theta) is injective on Θ\Theta. Since the moment equations are satisfied at the true parameter, injectivity then yields global identification of θ0\theta_{0} as the unique root of Ξ⁡(θ)=0\Xi(\theta)=0.
The implementation of this idea requires introducing the following covariate regions. Fix a constant B∈ℝ+⁣+B\in\mathbb{R}_{++} with B>1/2B>1/2. For each q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\} and ϵ>0\epsilon>0, let

𝒳q,ϵγ={x∈𝒳qr​e​g:\displaystyle\mathcal{X}^{\gamma}_{q,\epsilon}=\Big\{x\in\mathcal{X}_{q}^{reg}: ‖x‖∞<B,\displaystyle\ \norm{x}_{\infty}<B,
x1​q≥x3​q+ϵ3,x3​q≥x2​q+ϵ3,\displaystyle\ x_{1q}\geq x_{3q}+\frac{\epsilon}{3},\quad x_{3q}\geq x_{2q}+\frac{\epsilon}{3},
x2​r≥x3​r+ϵ3,x3​r≥x1​r+ϵ3,r∈{1,…,Q}∖{q},\displaystyle\ x_{2r}\geq x_{3r}+\frac{\epsilon}{3},\quad x_{3r}\geq x_{1r}+\frac{\epsilon}{3},\quad r\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}\setminus\{q\},
|xt​s,l|<ϵ,∀(t,s,l)∈{1,2,3}2×{1,…,Q}}\displaystyle\ \absolutevalue{x_{ts,l}}<\epsilon,\quad\forall(t,s,l)\in\{1,2,3\}^{2}\times\{1,\ldots,Q\}\Big\}

and let

𝒳qβ={x∈𝒳qr​e​g:\displaystyle\mathcal{X}^{\beta}_{q}=\Big\{x\in\mathcal{X}_{q}^{reg}: ‖x‖∞<B,\displaystyle\ \norm{x}_{\infty}<B,
x1​q>x3​q+12,x3​q>x2​q+12,\displaystyle\ x_{1q}>x_{3q}+\frac{1}{2},\quad x_{3q}>x_{2q}+\frac{1}{2},
x2​r>x3​r+12,x3​r>x1​r+12,r∈{1,…,Q}∖{q}}.\displaystyle\ x_{2r}>x_{3r}+\frac{1}{2},\quad x_{3r}>x_{1r}+\frac{1}{2},\quad r\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}\setminus\{q\}\Big\}.

where we use the shorthand xt​s,q=xt,q−xs,qx_{ts,q}=x_{t,q}-x_{s,q} for conciseness. The set 𝒳qβ\mathcal{X}^{\beta}_{q} can be thought of as identifying the common slope coefficient β\beta, while the sets 𝒳q,ϵγ\mathcal{X}^{\gamma}_{q,\epsilon} pin down the state-dependence parameters γq\gamma_{q}. These bounded covariate regions are constructed in such a way that the Jacobian of the identifying map, ∇Ξ​(θ)\nabla\Xi(\theta), possesses a particular sign and dominance structure. Specifically, for Ξ⁡(θ)\Xi(\theta) defined in (40), they imply that ∇Ξ​(θ)\nabla\Xi(\theta) has all entries positive and is strictly diagonally dominant, uniformly over θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, once ϵ1,…,ϵQ\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{Q} are chosen sufficiently small. The latter condition means that the relevant own-derivative terms dominate the cross-derivative terms in absolute value. Appendix Lemma 6 shows that these properties imply that ∇Ξ​(θ)\nabla\Xi(\theta) is a PP-matrix, as desired.

Proposition 1

Suppose that Assumptions 1-2 hold and that

P⁡(Y0=y0,X∈𝒳y0β)>0for all ​y0∈{1,…,Q}\displaystyle P(Y_{0}=y_{0},X\in\mathcal{X}^{\beta}_{y_{0}})>0\quad\text{for all }y_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,Q\} (38)
P⁡(Y0=y0,X∈𝒳y0,ϵγ)>0for all ​y0∈{1,…,Q}​ and ​ϵ∈(0,3​B)\displaystyle P(Y_{0}=y_{0},X\in\mathcal{X}^{\gamma}_{y_{0},\epsilon})>0\quad\text{for all }y_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}\text{ and }\epsilon\in(0,3B) (39)

Then, there exists ϵ1,…,ϵQ\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{Q}, sufficiently small positive constants, such that the mapping

Ξ⁡(θ)=(𝔼[my0σ1,1(Y,X,θ)|Y0=1,X∈𝒳β1]𝔼[my0σ1,1(Y,X,θ)|Y0=1,X∈𝒳γ1,ϵ1]𝔼[my0σ1,2(Y,X,θ)|Y0=2,X∈𝒳γ2,ϵ2]𝔼[my0σ1,Q(Y,X,θ)|Y0=Q,X∈𝒳γQ,ϵQ])\displaystyle\Xi(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{E}\left[m_{y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},1}(Y,X,\theta)|Y_{0}=1,X\in\mathcal{X}^{\beta}_{1}\right]\\ \mathbb{E}\left[m_{y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},1}(Y,X,\theta)|Y_{0}=1,X\in\mathcal{X}^{\gamma}_{1,\epsilon_{1}}\right]\\ \mathbb{E}\left[m_{y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},2}(Y,X,\theta)|Y_{0}=2,X\in\mathcal{X}^{\gamma}_{2,\epsilon_{2}}\right]\\ \vdots\\ \mathbb{E}\left[m_{y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},Q}(Y,X,\theta)|Y_{0}=Q,X\in\mathcal{X}^{\gamma}_{Q,\epsilon_{Q}}\right]\end{pmatrix} (40)

is injective on Θ\Theta. Thus, θ0\theta_{0} is the unique solution to Ξ⁡(θ)=0\Xi(\theta)=0, i.e., it is identified.

The proof is given in the Appendix. The use of the initial condition Y0=1Y_{0}=1 in the first component of Ξ⁡(θ)\Xi(\theta), which identifies β\beta, is inessential and could be replaced by any other initial condition.1616 16 Accordingly, (38) can be relaxed to there exists y0∈{1,…,Q}y_{0}\in\{1,\ldots,Q\} such that P⁡(Y0=y0,X∈𝒳y0β)>0P(Y_{0}=y_{0},X\in\mathcal{X}^{\beta}_{y_{0}})>0, without modification to the proof. By contrast, our proof recovers the state-dependence parameters by exploiting observations from each initial condition, which explains the support requirement in (39).
In sum, Proposition 1 establishes point identification of the parameter θ0\theta_{0} in the empirical specification (4) through the moment map Ξ⁡(θ)\Xi(\theta). Because these moments are evaluated over events with positive probability, the argument also shows that θ0\theta_{0} is, in principle, n\sqrt{n}-estimable. The particular map in (40), however, is best viewed as a constructive device for proving identification. Using it directly for estimation would require selecting the tuning constants ϵ1,…,ϵQ\epsilon_{1},\ldots,\epsilon_{Q} and restricting attention to small covariate regions, which would be cumbersome and generally inefficient. For this reason, our empirical application instead uses a tuning-parameter-free and more flexible GMM procedure based on the collection of moment functions in (19).

6 Empirical application

In this section, we illustrate the use of the moment conditions derived above for estimation of a simple model for product choice as a function of prices in the presence of state dependence and persistent unobserved heterogeneity. The product that we consider is soft drinks, and the parameters of interest are a common coefficient on price in the indirect utility function and product-specific coefficients on an indicator for whether the same product was chosen on the previous purchase occasion.

The data are from 2019 and come from NielsenIQ.1717 17 The results presented here are based on our own analyses calculated (or derived) based in part on data from Nielsen Consumer LLC and marketing databases provided through the NielsenIQ Datasets at the Kilts Center for Marketing Data Center at The University of Chicago Booth School of Business. The conclusions drawn from the NielsenIQ data are those of the researchers and do not reflect the views of NielsenIQ. NielsenIQ is not responsible for, had no role in, and was not involved in analyzing and preparing the results reported herein. There are 8,100 households making a total of 47,933 purchases of soft drinks. The categories are aggregated into Cola, Root Beer/Ginger Flavor, Citrus Flavor, Soft Drink with Unique Flavor, and Other. The households are located in one of the ten largest Nielsen DMAs. For each of the categories, we calculate the price as a weighted average of sales in all stores of the household Nielsen DMA within the week of purchase. In addition to household ID, option chosen and prices, we also have information on the Nielsen DMA, household income, household size and race.1818 18 A Designated Market Area (DMA) is a federally registered trademark and service mark of The Nielsen Company (US), LLC. Income is measured in intervals on the real line with cutoff at $5,000, $8,000, $10,000, $15,000, $20,000, $25,000, $30,000, $35,000, $40,000, $45,000, $50,000, $60,000, and $100,000. We record income as 2.5 for observations in the bottom interval and as 125 for observations in the top interval; for the remaining observations income is recorded at the midpoint of the interval divided by 1000. Table 2 displays summary statistics for the data.

Figure 1 shows the histogram of the number of purchases per household and Table 3 shows the number of transitions between products.

Table 3 shows substantial persistence in choices, with 59% of purchases repeating the previous category. However, persistence varies considerably by product. For example, 66% of cola purchases are followed by another cola purchase, while only 49% of citrus drink purchases are followed by citrus drinks. The large degree of persistence suggests that true state dependence and/or persistent unobserved preferences play an important role. These patterns motivate a model that allows for product-specific state dependence as well as unrestricted individual-product heterogeneity. Specifically, we consider the linear specification (4) with price as an explanatory variable. That is,

zt(q,yt−1,Price,θ)=Pricet,q×β+γq𝟙{yt−1=q}z_{t}(q,y_{t-1},\text{Price},\theta)=\text{Price}_{t,q}\times\beta+\gamma_{q}\mathbbm{1}\left\{y_{t-1}=q\right\}

where θ=(β′,γ1,…,γQ)′\theta=(\beta^{\prime},\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{Q})^{\prime}. In this model, the γq\gamma_{q}’s measure the product specific state dependence and the fixed effects Aq​iA_{qi} control unrestricted individual-product specific heterogeneity. Proposition 1 in the previous section established that θ\theta is identified under appropriate support conditions.

Let Zis:t=(Zi​s,Zi,s+1,…,Zi​t)Z_{i}^{s:t}=(Z_{is},Z_{i,s+1},\ldots,Z_{it}) for s<ts<t, and let TiT_{i} denote the number of observed purchase occasions for individual ii after the initial condition. We estimate the model by generalized method of moments (GMM), using as building blocks the three-period conditional moment functions displayed in (37). For every individual ii with Ti≥3T_{i}\geq 3, we exploit the moment functions associated with each consecutive three-period window. That is, for each soda category qq, the collection of conditional moment functions we consider is

mYi​0σ1,σ+,q(Yi1:3,Pricei1:3,θ),mYi​1σ1,σ+,q(Yi2:4,Pricei2:4,θ),…,mYi,Ti−3σ1,σ+,q(YiTi−2:Ti,PriceiTi−2:Ti,θ).\displaystyle m_{Y_{i0}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{+},q}\left(Y_{i}^{1:3},\mathrm{Price}_{i}^{1:3},\theta\right),\quad m_{Y_{i1}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{+},q}\left(Y_{i}^{2:4},\mathrm{Price}_{i}^{2:4},\theta\right),\quad\ldots,\quad m_{Y_{i,T_{i}-3}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{+},q}\left(Y_{i}^{T_{i}-2:T_{i}},\mathrm{Price}_{i}^{T_{i}-2:T_{i}},\theta\right).

Following Honoré and Weidner (2025), we first pre-normalize each conditional moment function by dividing it by the sum of the absolute values of the distinct summands appearing in its expression.1919 19 Appendix D.2 gives a disaggregated expression of mY0σ1,σ+,q​(Y,X,θ)m_{Y_{0}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{+},q}(Y,X,\theta), making explicit its constituent terms. This normalization uniformly bounds the conditional moment functions and their gradients over the parameter space. As in the binary choice setting considered by Honoré and Weidner (2025), we find that this rescaling improves the finite-sample performance of the resulting GMM estimators.

Next, we form unconditional moment functions by interacting the rescaled conditional moment functions m~Yi,s−1σ1,σ+,q(Yis:s+2,Priceis:s+2,θ)\widetilde{m}_{Y_{i,s-1}}^{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{+},q}\left(Y_{i}^{s:s+2},\mathrm{Price}_{i}^{s:s+2},\theta\right) with indicators for the initial condition Yi​s−1Y_{is-1} and the relative price differences Pricei​s,q′−Pricei​s,cola\mathrm{Price}_{is,q^{\prime}}-\mathrm{Price}_{is,\mathrm{cola}}, Pricei​s+1,q′−Pricei​s+1,cola\mathrm{Price}_{is+1,q^{\prime}}-\mathrm{Price}_{is+1,\mathrm{cola}}, and Pricei​s+2,q′−Pricei​s+2,cola\mathrm{Price}_{is+2,q^{\prime}}-\mathrm{Price}_{is+2,\mathrm{cola}} for each product category q′q^{\prime} other than cola.2020 20 Because only price differences matter in the multinomial logit model, we use prices relative to cola rather than price levels.

Finally, to keep the dimension of the estimating moment vector manageable, we sum up these unconditional moments across all three-period windows within each soda category qq, for each individual ii. This procedure ultimately yields a total of 85 moment conditions. Since this number is large relative to the sample size,2121 21 The weighting matrix has 3,655 unique elements, while the sample size is 36,859. estimating a fully unrestricted optimal weighting matrix may be unstable. We therefore use a two-step GMM procedure in which the second-step weighting matrix is diagonal, with each diagonal element equal to the inverse of the sample variance of the corresponding moment function evaluated at the initial GMM estimator.

The calculations in Section 4.3 above reveal that moment conditions derived from (26) can have heavy–tailed distributions. The results presented in Table 4 suggest that this is not an issue for the moments used in the estimation in this section. Specifically, Table 4 presents summary statistics for the empirical distribution of the 3-period conditional moment functions in equation (37) evaluated at the GMM estimator. Since each of the moments has a high probability of being 0, we present that probability along with summary statistics for the moment functions conditional on not being 0. Conditional on not being 0, all of the five moment functions have skewness close to 0 and the kurtosis is between 1.241.24 and 1.351.35. Consistent with equation (37), the minimum value is always −1-1, while the maximum value is below 2.52.5.

In addition to the GMM estimator based on the moments derived in this paper, we also calculate the maximum likelihood estimator of a multinomial logit models that uses prices, past choice, household size, household income, and race dummies as explanatory variables. The GMM estimation requires at least four purchase occasions for a household, while the multinomial logit maximum likelihood estimator only requires two. We therefore calculate maximum likelihood estimator on the sample of household with at least two purchases as well as for the data used for the GMM estimator. The results are reported in Table 5.

The maximum likelihood estimates that do not account for unobserved heterogeneity imply substantial state dependence, with coefficients between 1.5 and 2.5 depending on the product category. In contrast, the GMM estimates that control for fixed effects are dramatically smaller, ranging from 0.02 to 0.29. This difference suggests that a large share of the observed persistence in choices is due to persistent unobserved heterogeneity rather than true state dependence. After controlling for this heterogeneity, state dependence remains economically modest and is close to zero for some categories, such as citrus and other soft drinks. The large difference between the MLE and GMM estimates highlights the importance of controlling for unobserved heterogeneity when estimating state dependence in discrete choice models.

In contrast, the estimated price coefficient is remarkably stable across specifications, at approximately −0.11-0.11, suggesting that ignoring unobserved heterogeneity primarily biases estimates of state dependence rather than price sensitivity. At a superficial level, this is not surprising since the prices are plausibly independent of the household fixed effects.

7 Conclusion

This paper has shown how to produce moment conditions free of the fixed effects for the dynamic multinomial logit model. Our approach is based on a simple observation: permuting outcomes across time periods leaves the contribution of the alternative-specific fixed effects unchanged, so the ratio of a transformed-model probability which permutes the order of outcomes to the true-model probability is free of those effects. When the chosen permutation is cyclic, the transformed model defines a proper distribution. This alone yields a valid moment condition, and contrasting two such models delivers additional ones for the common parameters. The construction requires at least three time periods after the initial condition, and we provide an explicit formula for the number of linearly independent moments that are generated this way. This number grows quickly in both the number of alternatives and the number of time periods.

Two features of the construction of moment conditions in this paper are worth emphasizing. First, it is explicit. Unlike the abstract characterization obtained from functional differencing, our approach delivers moment functions in closed form that can be used directly for estimation. Second, the construction is general. The only model-specific ingredient is that the static counterpart of the model admits a sufficient statistic for the fixed effects that is symmetric in the time indices. Whenever such a sufficient statistic exists, the transformed-model device can be deployed to generate fixed effects-free moment conditions for the corresponding dynamic model with lagged dependent variables. This unifies the multinomial logit with other results, and provides one way to proceed in panel data settings that have not yet been studied.

We put our moment conditions to use in two ways. We establish point identification of the parameters in our empirical specification under support conditions that, unlike conditional-likelihood arguments, do not require covariates to be constant across periods. We also leverage the moment conditions to estimate a multinomial logit model with fixed effects in an application to household soft drink purchases. Accounting for unobserved heterogeneity in this application sharply reduces the estimated degree of state dependence relative to a model that ignores it, while leaving the price coefficient essentially unchanged. This suggests that much of the persistence in observed choices can be explained by stable unobserved preferences rather than genuine state dependence.

Several questions remain open. For example, our count of linearly independent moment conditions is supported by a proof for the binary case and otherwise for three time periods. We verified the validity of the claim numerically more broadly, but a general analytical proof for more than two alternatives is still lacking. Also, while the transformed-model moments are always valid, they need not be well behaved when applied in specific settings. As the linear panel data Gaussian example illustrates, they can be heavy–tailed in which case they may be best viewed as a constructive existence result that complements, rather than replaces, model-specific reasoning about how best to eliminate the fixed effects. Characterizing efficient or well-behaved combinations of the available moments, and extending the construction to richer forms of dependence and to settings without independence of irrelevant alternatives, are natural directions for future work.

Appendix A Discussion of Conjecture 1

This appendix discusses two complementary strategies for proving Conjecture 1. The first uses the polynomial structure of the model probabilities in the fixed effect parameter to derive a lower bound on the total number of linearly independent moment conditions, which together with a known matching upper bound pins down the count exactly for Q=2Q=2. The second argues directly about linear independence of the ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) moments in (24), which we establish rigorously for T=3T=3 and any Q≥2Q\geq 2.

where κ⁡(η)=[(∑r=1Qπ1​(r,y0)​ηr)​∏t=2T∏l=1Q(∑r=1Qπt​(r,l)​ηr)]−1\kappa(\eta)=\Big[\big(\sum_{r=1}^{Q}\pi_{1}(r,y_{0})\eta_{r}\big)\prod_{t=2}^{T}\prod_{l=1}^{Q}\big(\sum_{r=1}^{Q}\pi_{t}(r,l)\eta_{r}\big)\Big]^{-1} depends on η\eta but not on yy, and
