A.2 Strategy 2: linear independence of the moments in (24)

The second strategy works directly with the ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) explicit moment functions in (24). If these moments are linearly independent for generic (y0,x,θ)(y_{0},x,\theta), then at least ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) linearly independent moment conditions exist. Combined with a matching upper bound on that number, which is known for Q=2Q=2 (see Strategy 1), this establishes Conjecture 1.

We prove linear independence rigorously for T=3T=3 and any Q≥2Q\geq 2. For T=3T=3 and any Q≥2Q\geq 2, the moment functions m1,…,mQm_{1},\ldots,m_{Q} in (45) are linearly independent in ℝQT\mathbb{R}^{Q^{T}} for generic (y0,x,θ0)(y_{0},x,\theta_{0}).

Proposition 2 establishes the first half of Conjecture 1 (linear independence of the constructed moments) for T=3T=3 and any Q≥2Q\geq 2, and implies that at least ℓ⁡(Q,3)=Q\ell(Q,3)=Q linearly independent moment conditions of the form (8) exist for generic (y0,x,θ0)(y_{0},x,\theta_{0}). The second half of the conjecture (that every valid moment function is a linear combination of the constructed moments, equivalently that there are no more than ℓ⁡(Q,3)\ell(Q,3) linearly independent moment conditions) is supported by direct numerical computation for T=3T=3 but does not have a clean analytical proof for Q≥3Q\geq 3.

The obstacle for T≥4T\geq 4.

For T≥4T\geq 4, linear independence of the ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) moment functions in (24) has been verified by direct numerical computation for all values of (Q,T)(Q,T) in Table 1, but a general analytical proof has so far eluded us. A natural extension of the T=3T=3 argument groups the moments hierarchically by the number of shared time indices jj and, within each level, by the shared-position values 𝐭\mathbf{t} and 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Within a fixed group the moments reduce to a structure analogous to the T=3T=3 case, and a similar diagonal evaluation-point argument applies on a restricted slice of the outcome space. Combining the slices into a single linear-independence statement requires bookkeeping that we have not been able to carry out cleanly for arbitrary (Q,T)(Q,T).

A.3 Summary

Combining the two strategies, the count ℓ⁡(Q,T)\ell(Q,T) in Conjecture 1 is established analytically for Q=2Q=2 and any T≥3T\geq 3 (by Strategy 1) and, as a lower bound, for T=3T=3 and any Q≥2Q\geq 2 (by Strategy 2). For Q≥3Q\geq 3 the conjecture remains open in both halves: at T=3T=3 we have the lower bound but not exhaustiveness, and for T≥4T\geq 4 neither half is established. Equality has been verified numerically for all (Q,T)(Q,T) in Table 1 but not proved analytically. We leave a complete analytical proof of Conjecture 1 for future work.

Appendix B Generalized moment conditions for non-cyclic permutations

Theorem 1 constructs moment conditions from pairs of cyclic permutations σ1,σ2\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}. In this appendix, we show that the construction extends to pairs of general (not necessarily cyclic) permutations, provided they satisfy a compatibility condition on their cycle structures. In all cases we have checked numerically, the resulting moment conditions do not generate any linearly independent moments beyond those already obtained from cyclic permutations in Theorem 1, so this generalization is not needed for Conjecture 1. However, the result is of independent interest, as it clarifies the structure of the transformed model approach and may be useful for extensions to other models.

B.1 Transformed models for non-cyclic permutations

For a general (not necessarily cyclic) permutation σ:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\}, the transformed model pσp^{\sigma} defined in (11) does not correspond to a single Markov chain through all TT outcomes. Instead, pσp^{\sigma} factorizes as a product of independent Markov chains, one for each cycle of σ\sigma.

To see this, recall that every permutation σ\sigma can be decomposed into disjoint cycles. Let σ=c1∘c2∘⋯∘cL\sigma=c_{1}\circ c_{2}\circ\cdots\circ c_{L} be the cycle decomposition, with L≥1L\geq 1 cycles. Each cycle cℓc_{\ell} acts on a subset Cℓ⊂{1,…,T}C_{\ell}\subset\{1,\ldots,T\}, and {C1,…,CL}\{C_{1},\ldots,C_{L}\} is a partition of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\}. Let C∗C_{*} denote the cycle containing TT, and write C∗={T,σ⁡(T),σ2​(T),…,σ|C∗|−1​(T)}C_{*}=\{T,\sigma(T),\sigma^{2}(T),\ldots,\sigma^{|C_{*}|-1}(T)\}. For the cycle C∗C_{*}, define the generation order τ∗​(k):=σk​(T)\tau_{*}(k):=\sigma^{k}(T) for k=1,…,|C∗|k=1,\ldots,|C_{*}|, so that τ∗​(|C∗|)=T\tau_{*}(|C_{*}|)=T. Similarly, for each cycle CℓC_{\ell} not containing TT, pick any element aℓ∈Cℓa_{\ell}\in C_{\ell} and define the generation order within that cycle by τℓ​(k):=σk​(aℓ)\tau_{\ell}(k):=\sigma^{k}(a_{\ell}) for k=1,…,|Cℓ|k=1,\ldots,|C_{\ell}|, with τℓ​(|Cℓ|)=aℓ\tau_{\ell}(|C_{\ell}|)=a_{\ell}. In (46) below we also use the convention τℓ​(0):=aℓ\tau_{\ell}(0):=a_{\ell}, which reflects that this chain returns to its starting outcome.

The transformed model pσp^{\sigma} can then be written as

pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=p1​(yτ∗​(1)∣y0,x,θ,α)​∏k=2|C∗|pτ∗​(k−1)+1​(yτ∗​(k)∣yτ∗​(k−1),x,θ,α)⏟chain through cycle ​C∗\displaystyle p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=\underbrace{p_{1}(y_{\tau_{*}(1)}\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)\prod_{k=2}^{|C_{*}|}p_{\tau_{*}(k-1)+1}(y_{\tau_{*}(k)}\mid y_{\tau_{*}(k-1)},x,\theta,\alpha)}_{\text{chain through cycle }C_{*}} (46)
×∏ℓ:Cℓ≠C∗∏k=1|Cℓ|pτℓ​(k−1)+1​(yτℓ​(k)∣yτℓ​(k−1),x,θ,α)⏟chain through cycle ​Cℓ.\times\prod_{\ell:C_{\ell}\neq C_{*}}\underbrace{\prod_{k=1}^{|C_{\ell}|}p_{\tau_{\ell}(k-1)+1}(y_{\tau_{\ell}(k)}\mid y_{\tau_{\ell}(k-1)},x,\theta,\alpha)}_{\text{chain through cycle }C_{\ell}}.

Each factor in (46) is a Markov chain that generates the outcomes {ys:s∈Cℓ}\{y_{s}:s\in C_{\ell}\} independently of the outcomes in other cycles. For cycles Cℓ≠C∗C_{\ell}\neq C_{*}, the chain starts from the outcome yaℓy_{a_{\ell}}, which also appears as the outcome generated in the last step of the chain (since τℓ​(|Cℓ|)=aℓ\tau_{\ell}(|C_{\ell}|)=a_{\ell}). Hence, summing pσp^{\sigma} over all ysy_{s} with s∈Cℓs\in C_{\ell} for Cℓ≠C∗C_{\ell}\neq C_{*} does not yield one for generic (x,θ,α)(x,\theta,\alpha), because these chains are “closed loops” that both start and end at yaℓy_{a_{\ell}}.

Nevertheless, Lemma 2 continues to hold: the ratio Sy0σ​(y,x,θ)=pσ​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)/p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)S^{\sigma}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)=p^{\sigma}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)/p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha) is free of α\alpha for any permutation σ\sigma, not just cyclic ones. This is because the proof of Lemma 2 only uses the fact that σ\sigma is a permutation (so that ∑tαyσ⁡(t−1)=∑tαyt\sum_{t}\alpha_{y_{\sigma(t-1)}}=\sum_{t}\alpha_{y_{t}}), not that σ\sigma is cyclic.

B.2 Equivalence relation on permutations

We define an equivalence relation ∼\sim on the set of all permutations of {1,…,T}\{1,\ldots,T\} as follows.

Definition 1

Two permutations σ1,σ2:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} satisfy σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2} if and only if their cycle decompositions are identical except possibly for the cycles containing TT.

That is, σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2} if every cycle that does not contain TT appears identically in both σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2}. The cycles containing TT are allowed to differ but must have the same length. Note that σ∼σ\sigma\sim\sigma always holds.

For example, with T=7T=7, the permutations σ1=[1,5,3]​[2,4,7]​[6]\sigma_{1}=[1,5,3][2,4,7][6] and σ2=[1,5,3]​[2,7,4]​[6]\sigma_{2}=[1,5,3][2,7,4][6] satisfy σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2}, because the cycles [1,5,3][1,5,3] and [6][6] (which do not contain T=7T=7) are identical, while the cycles [2,4,7][2,4,7] and [2,7,4][2,7,4] (which contain T=7T=7) differ.

When σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2}, the two permutations share the same “non-TT cycles.” Denote their union by Cshared:=⋃ℓ:T∉CℓCℓC_{\mathrm{shared}}:=\bigcup_{\ell:T\notin C_{\ell}}C_{\ell}. Let C∗(1)C_{*}^{(1)} and C∗(2)C_{*}^{(2)} denote the cycles of σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} that contain TT, respectively. Since σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2}, we have C∗(1)=C∗(2)C_{*}^{(1)}=C_{*}^{(2)} as sets (both equal {1,…,T}∖Cshared\{1,\ldots,T\}\setminus C_{\mathrm{shared}}), though σ1\sigma_{1} and σ2\sigma_{2} may permute the elements of this set differently.

B.3 Shared index set

For two permutations σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2}, we now define the set of “shared indices” that determines the structure of the generalized moment conditions. Consider the generation orders within the cycles containing TT:

τ∗(1)(k):=σ1k(T),τ∗(2)(k):=σ2k(T),k=1,2,…,|C∗|.\displaystyle\tau_{*}^{(1)}(k):=\sigma_{1}^{k}(T),\qquad\tau_{*}^{(2)}(k):=\sigma_{2}^{k}(T),\qquad k=1,2,\ldots,|C_{*}|.

Since the two cycles contain the same set of elements C∗(1)=C∗(2)C_{*}^{(1)}=C_{*}^{(2)}, both generation orders are permutations of the same set, but they may list the elements in different orders. Additionally, the elements of CsharedC_{\mathrm{shared}} provide further shared indices from the non-TT cycles.

We define the shared index set as

ℐσ1,σ2:={(t,t):t∈Cshared}∪{(t,t):t=σ1j(T)=σ2j(T),j=1,…,k∗}∪{(s1,s2)},\displaystyle{\cal I}_{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}}:=\big\{(t,t):t\in C_{\mathrm{shared}}\big\}\cup\big\{(t,t):t=\sigma_{1}^{j}(T)=\sigma_{2}^{j}(T),\ j=1,\ldots,k^{*}\big\}\cup\big\{(s_{1},s_{2})\big\}, (47)

where the diagonal pairs (tk,tk)(t_{k},t_{k}) correspond to all elements in the shared non-TT cycles together with the elements on which the two generation orders through C∗C_{*} still agree, and (s1,s2)(s_{1},s_{2}) with s1≠s2s_{1}\neq s_{2} corresponds to the “split point” where the two cycles containing TT first diverge. More precisely, let k∗k^{*} be the largest integer such that τ∗(1)\tau_{*}^{(1)} and τ∗(2)\tau_{*}^{(2)} agree on their first k∗k^{*} entries:

σ1j(T)=σ2j(T),j=1,…,k∗,\displaystyle\sigma_{1}^{j}(T)=\sigma_{2}^{j}(T),\quad j=1,\ldots,k^{*},

and σ1k∗+1​(T)≠σ2k∗+1​(T)\sigma_{1}^{k^{*}+1}(T)\neq\sigma_{2}^{k^{*}+1}(T). Then s1=σ1k∗+1​(T)s_{1}=\sigma_{1}^{k^{*}+1}(T) and s2=σ2k∗+1​(T)s_{2}=\sigma_{2}^{k^{*}+1}(T), and the tkt_{k} from the TT-cycle are the shared elements σ1j​(T)=σ2j​(T)\sigma_{1}^{j}(T)=\sigma_{2}^{j}(T) for j=1,…,k∗j=1,\ldots,k^{*}. Let σ1,σ2:{1,…,T}→{1,…,T}\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}:\{1,\ldots,T\}\to\{1,\ldots,T\} be two permutations satisfying σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2} (Definition 1), with σ1≠σ2\sigma_{1}\neq\sigma_{2}. By Lemma 2 (which holds for all permutations, not just cyclic ones), we have Sy0σi​(y,x,θ)⋅p⁡(y∣y0,x,θ,α)=pσi​(y∣y0,x,θ,α)S^{\sigma_{i}}_{y_{0}}(y,x,\theta)\cdot p(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha)=p^{\sigma_{i}}(y\mid y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha) for i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}. ∑y∈{1,…,Q}T[{(yt1,…,yt[σ1,σ2])=q}pσ1(y)−{(yu1,…,yu[σ1,σ2])=q}pσ2(y)]=0,\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}^{T}}\left[\mathbbm{1}\!\left\{(y_{t_{1}},\ldots,y_{t_{[\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}]}})=q\right\}p^{\sigma_{1}}(y)-\mathbbm{1}\!\left\{(y_{u_{1}},\ldots,y_{u_{[\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}]}})=q\right\}p^{\sigma_{2}}(y)\right]=0, (50)

where we suppress the dependence on (y0,x,θ,α)(y_{0},x,\theta,\alpha) for brevity.

Step 1: Factorization of the transformed model over cycles. For any permutation σ\sigma with cycle decomposition σ=c1∘⋯∘cL\sigma=c_{1}\circ\cdots\circ c_{L}, the transformed model (15) can be written as a product over cycles:

The summation over {ys:s∈Cshared}\{y_{s}:s\in C_{\mathrm{shared}}\} is constrained by the indicators, and yields FsharedF_{\mathrm{shared}} evaluated at the fixed values. Fshared(q¯)⋅∑{ys:s∈C∗}{yσ1j​(T)=q¯j,j=1,…,k∗}[𝟙{ys1=q~}pC∗σ1(y)−𝟙{ys2=q~}pC∗σ2(y)],\displaystyle F_{\mathrm{shared}}(\bar{q})\cdot\sum_{\{y_{s}:s\in C_{*}\}}\mathbbm{1}\!\big\{y_{\sigma_{1}^{j}(T)}=\bar{q}_{j},\,j=1,\ldots,k^{*}\big\}\left[\mathbbm{1}\{y_{s_{1}}=\tilde{q}\}\,p^{\sigma_{1}}_{C_{*}}(y)-\mathbbm{1}\{y_{s_{2}}=\tilde{q}\}\,p^{\sigma_{2}}_{C_{*}}(y)\right],

where Fshared​(q¯)F_{\mathrm{shared}}(\bar{q}) absorbs the shared-cycle contributions.

Step 4: Telescoping within the TT-cycle. It remains to show that for each i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\},

Hi:=∑{ys:s∈C∗}{yσij​(T)=q¯j,j=1,…,k∗} 1{ysi=q~}pC∗σi(y)\displaystyle H_{i}:=\sum_{\{y_{s}:s\in C_{*}\}}\mathbbm{1}\!\big\{y_{\sigma_{i}^{j}(T)}=\bar{q}_{j},\,j=1,\ldots,k^{*}\big\}\,\mathbbm{1}\{y_{s_{i}}=\tilde{q}\}\,p^{\sigma_{i}}_{C_{*}}(y)

is the same for i=1i=1 and i=2i=2. Within the TT-cycle, pC∗σi​(y)p^{\sigma_{i}}_{C_{*}}(y) is a product of transition probabilities along the generation order τ∗(i)\tau_{*}^{(i)}. Hi=p1​(q¯1∣y0)​∏j=2k∗pσij−1​(T)+1​(q¯j∣q¯j−1)⋅pσik∗​(T)+1​(q~∣q¯k∗),\displaystyle H_{i}=p_{1}\!\left(\bar{q}_{1}\mid y_{0}\right)\prod_{j=2}^{k^{*}}p_{\sigma_{i}^{j-1}(T)+1}\!\left(\bar{q}_{j}\mid\bar{q}_{j-1}\right)\cdot p_{\sigma_{i}^{k^{*}}(T)+1}\!\left(\tilde{q}\mid\bar{q}_{k^{*}}\right),

Example: T=4T=4 with non-cyclic permutations. For T=4T=4, consider σ1=[1,2,4]​[3]\sigma_{1}=[1,2,4][3] and σ2=[1,4,2]​[3]\sigma_{2}=[1,4,2][3] (in sequence form, σ1=(2,4,3,1)\sigma_{1}=(2,4,3,1) and σ2=(4,1,3,2)\sigma_{2}=(4,1,3,2)). Both share the cycle [3][3] (which does not contain T=4T=4), and differ in the cycle containing 44: [1,2,4][1,2,4] versus [1,4,2][1,4,2]. Since neither σ1\sigma_{1} nor σ2\sigma_{2} is a cyclic permutation of {1,2,3,4}\{1,2,3,4\}, the moment conditions from Theorem 2 cannot be obtained directly from Theorem 1. The shared index set is ℐσ1,σ2={(3,3),(1,2)}{\cal I}_{\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}}=\{(3,3),(1,2)\}, with [σ1,σ2]=2[\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2}]=2, and the corresponding moment conditions are

𝔼[𝟙{Y1=q}SY0σ1(Y,X,θ0)−𝟙{Y2=q}SY0σ2(Y,X,θ0)|Y3,Y0,X,A]=0,\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{1}=q\}\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})-\mathbbm{1}\{Y_{2}=q\}\,S^{\sigma_{2}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})\,\Big|\,Y_{3},Y_{0},X,A\right]=0, (52)

for q∈{1,…,Q}q\in\{1,\ldots,Q\}. We now verify (52) directly using the chain representation.

The cycle C∗={1,2,4}C_{*}=\{1,2,4\} contains T=4T=4, and the shared cycle is {3}\{3\}. For σ1\sigma_{1}, the generation order within C∗C_{*} is τ∗(1)=(1,2,4)\tau_{*}^{(1)}=(1,2,4), meaning the chain visits y1y_{1}, then y2y_{2}, then y4y_{4}. For σ2\sigma_{2}, the generation order is τ∗(2)=(2,1,4)\tau_{*}^{(2)}=(2,1,4), visiting y2y_{2}, then y1y_{1}, then y4y_{4}. The shared cycle {3}\{3\} is a fixed point, producing a closed-loop factor. Using the chain representation from Section B.1, the transformed models are

pσ1​(y)\displaystyle p^{\sigma_{1}}(y) =p1​(y1∣y0)⋅p2​(y2∣y1)⋅p3​(y4∣y2)⏟chain through ​C∗={1,2,4}⋅p4​(y3∣y3)⏟loop at ​{3},\displaystyle=\underbrace{p_{1}(y_{1}\mid y_{0})\cdot p_{2}(y_{2}\mid y_{1})\cdot p_{3}(y_{4}\mid y_{2})}_{\text{chain through }C_{*}=\{1,2,4\}}\cdot\underbrace{p_{4}(y_{3}\mid y_{3})}_{\text{loop at }\{3\}},
pσ2​(y)\displaystyle p^{\sigma_{2}}(y) =p1​(y2∣y0)⋅p3​(y1∣y2)⋅p2​(y4∣y1)⏟chain through ​C∗={1,2,4}⋅p4​(y3∣y3)⏟loop at ​{3}.\displaystyle=\underbrace{p_{1}(y_{2}\mid y_{0})\cdot p_{3}(y_{1}\mid y_{2})\cdot p_{2}(y_{4}\mid y_{1})}_{\text{chain through }C_{*}=\{1,2,4\}}\cdot\underbrace{p_{4}(y_{3}\mid y_{3})}_{\text{loop at }\{3\}}.

The closed-loop factor p4​(y3∣y3)p_{4}(y_{3}\mid y_{3}) is identical in both expressions, as guaranteed by σ1∼σ2\sigma_{1}\sim\sigma_{2}.

Using Sσi⋅p=pσiS^{\sigma_{i}}\cdot p=p^{\sigma_{i}}, the moment condition (52) is equivalent to showing that for all α\alpha and for fixed y3y_{3},

∑y1,y2,y4𝟙{y1=q}pσ1(y)=∑y1,y2,y4𝟙{y2=q}pσ2(y).\displaystyle\sum_{y_{1},y_{2},y_{4}}\mathbbm{1}\{y_{1}=q\}\,p^{\sigma_{1}}(y)=\sum_{y_{1},y_{2},y_{4}}\mathbbm{1}\{y_{2}=q\}\,p^{\sigma_{2}}(y). (53)

The common factor p4​(y3∣y3)p_{4}(y_{3}\mid y_{3}) cancels from both sides. For the left-hand side, we sum the C∗C_{*}-chain of σ1\sigma_{1} over the free variables. Sum over y4y_{4} first (the last outcome generated by the chain):

∑y4p3​(y4∣y2)=1(telescopes).\displaystyle\sum_{y_{4}}p_{3}(y_{4}\mid y_{2})=1\qquad\text{(telescopes)}.

Then sum over y2y_{2}:

∑y2p2​(y2∣y1)=1(telescopes).\displaystyle\sum_{y_{2}}p_{2}(y_{2}\mid y_{1})=1\qquad\text{(telescopes)}.

What remains is ∑y1𝟙{y1=q}⋅p1(y1∣y0)=p1(q∣y0)\sum_{y_{1}}\mathbbm{1}\{y_{1}=q\}\cdot p_{1}(y_{1}\mid y_{0})=p_{1}(q\mid y_{0}).

For the right-hand side, we sum the C∗C_{*}-chain of σ2\sigma_{2} analogously. Sum over y4y_{4}:

∑y4p2​(y4∣y1)=1(telescopes).\displaystyle\sum_{y_{4}}p_{2}(y_{4}\mid y_{1})=1\qquad\text{(telescopes)}.

Then sum over y1y_{1}:

∑y1p3​(y1∣y2)=1(telescopes).\displaystyle\sum_{y_{1}}p_{3}(y_{1}\mid y_{2})=1\qquad\text{(telescopes)}.

What remains is ∑y2𝟙{y2=q}⋅p1(y2∣y0)=p1(q∣y0)\sum_{y_{2}}\mathbbm{1}\{y_{2}=q\}\cdot p_{1}(y_{2}\mid y_{0})=p_{1}(q\mid y_{0}).

Both sides equal p1​(q∣y0)p_{1}(q\mid y_{0}), confirming (53). The key mechanism is that both chains start from y0y_{0} (via the p1p_{1} factor) and visit the same set of outcomes {y1,y2,y4}\{y_{1},y_{2},y_{4}\}, but in different orders. When summing over all the free variables, the intermediate transitions telescope to one, and only the initial transition probability p1​(q∣y0)p_{1}(q\mid y_{0}) survives — regardless of the order in which the chain visits the elements.

Appendix C Details for the general exponential–family, bivariate gamma, and linear–normal examples

Lemma 4 states the sufficient statistic for the exponential–family model (28) discussed in Section 4, and Proposition 3 verifies the validity of the moment condition obtained from Lemma 3.

Lemma 4

(Sufficient statistic for the exponential–family model). Let (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) be independent with densities f⁡(yt,ηt,α)f(y_{t},\eta_{t},\alpha) given by (28), for indices η1,…,ηT\eta_{1},\ldots,\eta_{T} and common fixed effect α\alpha. Then S⁡(Y)=∑t=1Ts⁡(Yt)S(Y)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}s(Y_{t}) is sufficient for α\alpha, and the conditional distribution of (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}) given S=s¯S=\bar{s} does not depend on α\alpha:

f⁡(y∣S=s¯,x;θ)=exp⁡(∑t=1Tb⁡(yt,ηt,θ))∫𝒜s¯exp⁡(∑t=1Tb⁡(ut,ηt,θ))​𝑑u,𝒜s¯={u:∑ts⁡(ut)=s¯}.f(y\mid S=\bar{s},x;\theta)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}b(y_{t},\eta_{t},\theta)\big)}{\displaystyle\int_{\mathcal{A}_{\bar{s}}}\exp\!\big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}b(u_{t},\eta_{t},\theta)\big)\,du},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{\bar{s}}=\Big\{u:\textstyle\sum_{t}s(u_{t})=\bar{s}\Big\}. (54)

Moreover SS is symmetric in its arguments.

Proof. By (28), the joint density factors as

∏t=1Tf⁡(yt,ηt,α)=exp⁡(α′​e​(θ)​S​(y))⋅exp⁡(∑t=1Td⁡(ηt,α,θ))⋅exp⁡(∑t=1Tb⁡(yt,ηt,θ)),\prod_{t=1}^{T}f(y_{t},\eta_{t},\alpha)=\exp\!\big(\alpha^{\prime}e(\theta)\,S(y)\big)\cdot\exp\!\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}d(\eta_{t},\alpha,\theta)\Big)\cdot\exp\!\Big(\sum_{t=1}^{T}b(y_{t},\eta_{t},\theta)\Big),

with S⁡(y)=∑ts⁡(yt)S(y)=\sum_{t}s(y_{t}). The first factor depends on yy only through S⁡(y)S(y), and the second is free of yy. Conditioning on S=s¯S=\bar{s} divides by the integral of the joint over 𝒜s¯\mathcal{A}_{\bar{s}}; the factor exp⁡(α′​e​(θ)​s¯)\exp(\alpha' e(\theta)\,\bar s), which is constant on 𝒜s¯\mathcal{A}_{\bar{s}}, and the yy–free factor exp⁡(∑td⁡(ηt,α,θ))\exp(\sum_t d(\eta_t,\alpha,\theta)) cancel between numerator and denominator, leaving (54), which is free of α\alpha. Finally, S=∑ts⁡(Yt)S=\sum_{t}s(Y_{t}) is a sum and is therefore symmetric in (Y1,…,YT)(Y_{1},\ldots,Y_{T}).  

Proposition 3

(Moment conditions for the exponential–family panel model). Consider the dynamic model (27) with period densities (28) and T=3T=3. Then for any bounded gg,

𝔼[g(Y2)SY0σ1(Y,X,θ0)−g(Y1)|Y0,X,A]=0,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,g(Y_{2})\,S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}(Y,X,\theta_{0})-g(Y_{1})\;\Big|\;Y_{0},X,A\,\right]=0, (55)

where SY0σ1S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}} is given by (29) at θ=θ0\theta=\theta_{0}.

Proof. By Lemma 3, SY0σ1​p=pσ1S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}\,p=p^{\sigma_{1}}, so

Remark 2

The argument is structurally identical to the proof of Lemma 1 for the discrete case. The Markov property ensures that ηt\eta_{t} depends on yt−1y_{t-1} but not on yty_{t}. As a result, the reverse–cyclic permutation places each YtY_{t} as a free integration variable while its density parameter ηt\eta_{t} is governed by a different element of the triple, allowing each factor to integrate to unity independently. Summation in the discrete case is replaced by integration, and the indicator 𝟏{Yτ⁡(k)=q}\mathbf{1}\{Y_{\tau(k)}=q\} is replaced by the weighting function gg evaluated at Yτ⁡(k)Y_{\tau(k)}.

The bivariate gamma model (31) illustrates a model whose symmetric sufficient statistic depends on the common parameter, and therefore lies outside Hahn’s class. We record the corresponding sufficient statistic and moment condition.

(Moment conditions for the bivariate gamma model). For the dynamic model (31) with T=3T=3, the moment condition (33) holds for every bounded gg, with SY0σ1S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}} given by (32).

C.1 Moments of the linear–normal moment function

The discussion of the linear panel data model in Section 4 noted that the moment function (35) is the exponential of a quadratic form in the Gaussian outcomes. It is therefore heavy–tailed, with conditional moments that exist only when the state–dependence coefficient lies in a bounded interval. This appendix section makes the claim in Footnote 13 precise. The results build on Chapter 3 of Mathai and Provost (1992) which establishes that if W∼N⁡(μ,Σ)W\sim N(\mu,\Sigma) in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, CC is symmetric, and b∈ℝnb\in\mathbb{R}^{n} then

E[exp(W′CW+b′W)k]=det⁡(I−2​k​Σ​C)−1/2exp(12vk′Pk−1vk−12μ′Σ−1μ),\;E\!\left[\exp\!\big(W^{\prime}CW+b^{\prime}W\big)^{k}\right]=\det(I-2k\Sigma C)^{-1/2}\,\exp\!\Big(\tfrac{1}{2}\,v_{k}^{\prime}P_{k}^{-1}v_{k}-\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mu^{\prime}\Sigma^{-1}\mu\Big),\; (56)

where

Pk=Σ−1−2​k​C,vk=k​b+Σ−1​μ.P_{k}=\Sigma^{-1}-2kC,\qquad v_{k}=kb+\Sigma^{-1}\mu.

The kk-th moment is finite if and only if Σ−1−2​k​C\Sigma^{-1}-2kC is positive definite.

Take the linear index zt​(yt−1,x,θ)=γ​yt−1+xt′​βz_{t}(y_{t-1},x,\theta)=\gamma\,y_{t-1}+x_{t}^{\prime}\beta, so that (34) is the Gaussian first–order autoregressive model with a fixed effect, and let T=3T=3 with σ1\sigma_{1} the reverse cycle. Writing Sy0σ1=exp⁡(Q⁡(y)/σ2)S^{\sigma_{1}}_{y_{0}}=\exp\!\big(Q(y)/\sigma^{2}\big), expression (35) gives

Q⁡(y)=z1​(y2−y1)+z2​(y3−y2)+z3​(y1−y3),withzt=γ​yt−1+xt′​β.Q(y)=z_{1}(y_{2}-y_{1})+z_{2}(y_{3}-y_{2})+z_{3}(y_{1}-y_{3}),\quad\text{with}\quad z_{t}=\gamma y_{t-1}+x_{t}^{\prime}\beta. (57)

Expanding and collecting terms, the cross terms in y1​y2y_{1}y_{2} cancel, leaving

Q⁡(y)=γ​y3​(y1−y2)⏟quadratic+γ​y0​(y2−y1)+β′​[x1​(y2−y1)+x2​(y3−y2)+x3​(y1−y3)]⏟linear in ​y.Q(y)=\underbrace{\gamma\,y_{3}(y_{1}-y_{2})}_{\text{quadratic}}\;+\;\underbrace{\gamma\,y_{0}(y_{2}-y_{1})+\beta^{\prime}\big[x_{1}(y_{2}-y_{1})+x_{2}(y_{3}-y_{2})+x_{3}(y_{1}-y_{3})\big]}_{\text{linear in }y}. (58)

Conditional on (Y0,X,A)(Y_{0},X,A), the recursion Yt=γ​Yt−1+xt′​β+A+εtY_{t}=\gamma Y_{t-1}+x_{t}^{\prime}\beta+A+\varepsilon_{t} reads J​Y=μ0+εJY=\mu_{0}+\varepsilon with ε∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​I3)\varepsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{3}), so YY is normal with finite mean and variance σ2​P−1\sigma^{2}P^{-1}, where

P=(1+γ2−γ0−γ1+γ2−γ0−γ1).P=\begin{pmatrix}1+\gamma^{2}&-\gamma&0\\ -\gamma&1+\gamma^{2}&-\gamma\\ 0&-\gamma&1\end{pmatrix}.

Writing MM for the Hessian of QQ, so that its quadratic part is 12​y′​M​y\tfrac{1}{2}\,y^{\prime}My,

M=(00γ00−γγ−γ0),M=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\gamma\\ 0&0&-\gamma\\ \gamma&-\gamma&0\end{pmatrix},

and noting that QQ has no term that is constant in yy, we can write (SY0σ1)k=exp⁡(Y′​12​σ2​M​Y+b′​Y)k\big(S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}\big)^{k}=\exp\!\big(Y^{\prime}\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}M\,Y+b^{\prime}Y\big)^{k}, with b∈ℝ3b\in\mathbb{R}^{3} collecting the linear coefficients of Q/σ2Q/\sigma^{2}. This is exactly the form to which the result in (56) applies, with Σ=σ2​P−1\Sigma=\sigma^{2}P^{-1} and C=12​σ2​MC=\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}M. Equation (56) then tells us that the moment is finite when Σ−1−2​k⋅12​σ2​M=σ−2​(P−k​M)\Sigma^{-1}-2k\cdot\tfrac{1}{2\sigma^{2}}M=\sigma^{-2}\,(P-kM) is positive definite, i.e. when P−k​MP-kM is positive definite. Finiteness is therefore governed by γ\gamma alone, and not by σ2\sigma^{2}, AA, Y0Y_{0}, or XX.

It remains to turn positive definiteness of P−k​MP-kM into a condition on γ\gamma. The two leading principal minors of P−k​MP-kM are 1+γ21+\gamma^{2} and 1+γ2+γ41+\gamma^{2}+\gamma^{4}. So positive definiteness comes down to the sign of the full determinant. A direct computation gives

det⁡(P−k​M)=1−2​k​(k−1)​γ2​(1−γ+γ2),\det(P-kM)=1-2k(k-1)\,\gamma^{2}\big(1-\gamma+\gamma^{2}\big),

so 𝔼[(SY0σ1)k∣Y0,X,A]<∞\mathbb{E}\big[(S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}})^{k}\mid Y_{0},X,A\big]<\infty if and only if 2​k​(k−1)​γ2​(1−γ+γ2)<12k(k-1)\,\gamma^{2}(1-\gamma+\gamma^{2})<1.

For k=1k=1 the condition is satisfied for all γ\gamma; this is consistent with 𝔼[SY0σ1∣Y0,X,A]=1\mathbb{E}[S^{\sigma_{1}}_{Y_{0}}\mid Y_{0},X,A]=1. The second moment (k=2k=2) requires γ\gamma to lie between the two real roots of 1−4​γ2+4​γ3−4​γ41-4\gamma^{2}+4\gamma^{3}-4\gamma^{4}, that is γ∈(−0.400, 0.575)\gamma\in(-0.400,\,0.575), and the higher moments require the successively smaller intervals

Appendix D Proof of Proposition 1

Theorem 3, stated in Subsection D.1, restates Theorem 4 of Gale and Nikaido (1965) and is included for convenience. This result is the key tool used to establish point identification of θ0\theta_{0} for our empirical specification (4) in Proposition 1. Lemma 6 complements the theorem by providing simple sufficient conditions for a matrix to be a PP-matrix, the main condition required to apply Theorem 3. Subsection D.2 then gives a detailed proof of Proposition 1.

D.1 Auxiliary results

Theorem 3

(Theorem 4 in Gale and Nikaido (1965)). If Ξ:Θ↦ℝQ+1\Xi:\Theta\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{Q+1}, where Θ\Theta is a closed rectangular region of ℝQ+1\mathbb{R}^{Q+1}, is a differentiable mapping such that the jacobian matrix ∇Ξ​(θ)\nabla\Xi(\theta) is a P-matrix for all θ∈Θ\theta\in\Theta, then Ξ\Xi is univalent in Θ\Theta.

Lemma 6

Let J∈ℝn×nJ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}. Suppose that (i) Ji​j>0J_{ij}>0 for all i,j∈{1,…,n}i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}, and (ii) that JJ is strictly diagonally dominant, i.e.

∀i∈{1,…,n}:Ji​i>∑j≠iJi​j\displaystyle\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:\quad J_{ii}>\sum_{j\neq i}J_{ij}

Then JJ is a PP-matrix (that is, has all principal minors positive).

Proof. If J∈ℝn×nJ\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n} satisfies (i) and (ii), then it is clear that any principal submatrix of JJ also satisfies (i) and (ii). Therefore, it suffices to show that (i) and (ii) imply that det​(J)>0\text{det}(J)>0.

To this end, it is useful to write J=D+RJ=D+R where D=diag​(J11,…,Jn​n)D=\text{diag}(J_{11},\ldots,J_{nn}). Since det​(D)=∏i=1nJi​i>0\text{det}(D)=\prod\limits_{i=1}^{n}J_{ii}>0 by (i), DD is invertible and we can further write J=D⁡(I+D−1​R)J=D(I+D^{-1}R). Since det​(J)=det​(D)×det​(I+D−1​R)\text{det}(J)=\text{det}(D)\times\text{det}(I+D^{-1}R), the sign of det​(J)\text{det}(J) is determined by that of det​(I+D−1​R)\text{det}(I+D^{-1}R). By (ii), D−1​RD^{-1}R has row-sums strictly less than 1. Hence, by the Gershgorin disc theorem (e.g Theorem 6.1.1 Horn and Johnson (2012)), all eigenvalues of D−1​RD^{-1}R have moduli strictly less than one. It follows that any real eigenvalue of (I+D−1​R)(I+D^{-1}R) is strictly positive and thus contributes positively to det​(I+D−1​R)\text{det}(I+D^{-1}R). Furthermore, since (I+D−1​R)∈ℝn×n(I+D^{-1}R)\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, any of its complex eigenvalues admits a conjugate pair, and that pair contributes positively to det​(I+D−1​R)\text{det}(I+D^{-1}R). This establishes that det​(I+D−1​R)>0\text{det}(I+D^{-1}R)>0 which concludes the proof.
